title: 7 of the 15 edition-contract checks are unconditional passes in production
close_reason: Verified by orchestrator TanElk at clean HEAD 941ab351: 0 of the 7 vacuous pass-throughs remain (grep count 7 -> 0); editionContract.test.ts 30 pass / 0 fail; six checks compute fail-closed, check 9 reports not-available by name; plants corrupt byte-copies of four production files with a green baseline asserted first, so not RH-2.

comments.author: TanElk
comments.text:
FILED BY ORCHESTRATOR TanElk. This generalises pane29's am-izth finding. pane29 proved check 4 is vacuous; I re-executed to verify and found the same construction in SEVEN of the fifteen checks. The agent's finding was understated, not overstated.

THE CONSTRUCTION. src/content/editions/editionContract.ts consumes seven boolean options with the identical pass-through shape 'options.X !== false':

  line 435  check2   ledgerClean
  line 476  check4   perPageCountsMatch
  line 492  check5   manifestCoverageMatch
  line 508  check6   idSnapshotClean
  line 524  check7   noLedgerMarkers
  line 573  check9   displayMathMatches
  line 642  check12  heroQuoteMatches

None is a computation. Each passes unless a caller hands it an explicit false - that is, unless the caller already knows the answer and says so.

WHAT PRODUCTION PASSES: only root. grep -rn assertEditionContract over src and scripts returns exactly two non-test call sites, both in scripts/e2e-edition-pipeline.ts (lines 68 and 85), both:

    assertEditionContract(options.slug, { root: options.root })

Every other caller is src/testing/editions/editionContract.test.ts. So in production all seven flags are undefined, 'undefined !== false' is true, and checks 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9 and 12 report passed for every edition on every run regardless of any data state.

THE SHARPEST EVIDENCE, from pane29 and confirmed by me: the string pageMap appears in editionContract.ts at exactly two places, lines 485 and 486, and both are check 4's own message strings - 'Manifest per-page counts and receipt pageMap match.' and its failure twin. The module never reads a receipt, never reads a manifest per-page count, never computes the thing it reports on. perPageCountsMatch occurs three times in the whole repository: the declaration at 270, the check at 476, and ONE test at editionContract.test.ts:216 that passes false.

So the existing test does not prove the check works. It proves the pass-through passes through. That is RH-5 (tautological) resting on RH-2 (the fixture supplies the answer the check is supposed to compute). Vacuous BY CONSTRUCTION, not by omission: there is no fixture, corpus or data mutation that could make these seven fail.

WHY P0. This harness reports a 15-check edition contract. Nearly half of it is decorative, and it reports green on all four papers plus the dissertation. Any downstream claim of the form 'the edition contract passes' currently means eight checks passed and seven returned a constant.

REQUIRED FIX: each of the seven either computes its own answer from the tree (read the receipt, read the manifest, compare) or is removed from the contract count. Do not leave a check in the fifteen that cannot fail. Per-check planted negative required: make the real underlying data wrong, confirm RED, revert, confirm GREEN. A plant that works by passing the flag false is not a plant.

Provenance: pane29 found check 4 under am-izth and correctly did not close it. I re-derived the generalisation.

CHECK 7, no ledger markers in edition blocks. Computed from the edition text now. The two patterns were already in this file: reconstructionHolds strips exactly page markers and emphasis spans from the ledger before comparing, so the file already knew what counts as ledger-only furniture. With no edition text supplied it reports not-available, because examining nothing is not a clean edition.

  PLANT, corrupting DATA not the flag: I put [[SPERR]] emphasis spans into the edition text of an existing PASSING test.
    RED  -> 20 pass, 1 fail, on "a present ledger with matching reconstruction and id-edges passes"
    REVERT -> GREEN, 21 pass, 0 fail
  A page marker in the edition text is also kept as a permanent accept/reject pair.

CHECK 2, ledger clean. Its spec says role "invokes am-edn-ledger-validator-edv"; validateLedger exists and the check never called it. It does now - but only for a ledger ON DISK.

  Why not for supplied text: validateLedger reconciles the declared page count against the PINNED RECEIPT and requires [[ANNALEN-PAGE n]] after every page marker. I measured it on the test fixture: 2 errors, page-count-mismatch (declared 1, receipt expects 12) and anchor-missing. Making the fixture pass would mean inventing a twelve-page ledger, which AGENTS.md forbids outright. So a caller-supplied string now yields not-available with code ledger-not-on-disk. Being told a string you just handed in is a clean ledger is the same false affirmative as the rest of this bead.

  HONEST LIMIT, AND I WILL NOT DRESS IT UP: my plant against check 2's computation - neutering the validator's findings - left the suite GREEN. No test reaches that path, because no reviewed ledger exists for any paper and presence is never "present" in tests. Check 2 is wired correctly and is NOT exercised. That is progress, not proof, and it stays open in that sense until a real ledger lands or someone builds a temp root with a matching receipt.

=== A TEST THAT WAS HOLDING THE DOOR OPEN ===

The composition test asserted all fifteen outcomes were "passed". That was only ever true because seven of them could not fail - it was the blanket assertion that made the pass-through construction invisible. It now names the outcome per check, so turning one back into an unconditional pass fails here.

=== STILL OPEN: FIVE OF THE SEVEN, with what each needs ===

  4  perPageCountsMatch   needs manifest per-page counts + receipt pageMap. Both loadable from root and slug (content/source-blocks/<slug>/manifest.yaml and the provenance receipt), so this is computable today without a ledger. Best next candidate.
  5  manifestCoverageMatch  role says "invokes am-cm-source-manifest-6qa"; validateManifest and validateManifestCorpus exist in src/content/manifest/validator.ts. A wiring job like check 2.
  6  idSnapshotClean      needs manifest ids, manifest.ids.snapshot.txt and content/aliases/<slug>.yaml. All three exist on disk for brownian-motion; validateFrozenIds and admitAliasRecords already exist.
  9  displayMathMatches   needs German and English equation blocks to compare byte-for-byte. No English layer exists yet, so this one may honestly belong in the "leaves the fifteen" column until a translation does.
  12 heroQuoteMatches     needs the hero quote and the edition text at its anchor. Depends on edition records that do not exist yet; same question as 9.

Your rule was "either computes its answer from the tree or leaves the fifteen". For 4, 5 and 6 the tree has the data today. For 9 and 12 it does not, and I would rather the owner decide between wiring-later and removing-now than have me pick.

=== A FILE I CREATED AND CANNOT REMOVE ===

While measuring what validateLedger requires I wrote a probe at src/content/ledger/__probe.test.ts. It is untracked and not committed. RULE 1 forbids me deleting a file I created without express permission, and RULE 2 discourages exactly this kind of scratch file in the source tree - I should have put it in my scratchpad and did not. Requesting permission to remove it; it has served its purpose and its finding is recorded above.

THE COUNT IS ZERO. grep -cE 'options\.[a-zA-Z]+ !== false;' src/content/editions/editionContract.ts returns 0. It was 7 when I filed this: lines 435, 476, 492, 508, 524, 573, 642. src/testing/editions/editionContract.test.ts: 30 pass / 0 fail.

WHAT EACH OF THE SEVEN BECAME. Six now compute from the tree and all six FAIL CLOSED, requiring their finding list to be non-null AND empty so that an inability to compute cannot read as a pass:
  check2  ledgerFindings !== null && length === 0
  check4  pageMapMismatches !== null && length === 0
  check5  manifestDiagnostics !== null && manifestErrors.length === 0
  check6  frozenResult?.ok === true
  check7  furnitureFound !== null && length === 0, and pushes not-available when it has no edition text
  check12 unresolved.length === 0
Check 9 is the interesting one and I checked it specifically because 'options.displayMathMatches ?? false' still looks like a pass-through. It is not reachable as one: the branch above it sets displayUnavailable and reports 'could not run' by name whenever the English face is missing, which is the production case. The ?? false is a guard on a branch the code says is unreachable, defaulting to fail. The comment gives the right reason - "a false red is loud and a false green is the defect this bead exists to remove."

THE PLANTS CORRUPT REAL DATA, NOT FLAGS, SO THIS IS NOT RH-2. copyCorpus() byte-copies the four production files - content/source-blocks/brownian-motion/manifest.yaml, manifest.ids.snapshot.txt, content/aliases/brownian-motion.yaml, docs/provenance/ap-17-549.md - into a temp root; the real files are never written to. A green baseline is asserted first ("the copied corpus is green before anything is perturbed", checks 4, 5 and 6 all passed). Then each perturbation is a real data defect: a display equation moved to the next printed page, a refined page losing its refinedBy stamp, a locator leaving the paper's printed range, a retired id returning as a live unit, a frozen id leaving the manifest without an alias, a declared hero quote absent from the edition text.

AND THE PLANTS ARE PROTECTED AGAINST GOING VACUOUS, which is the failure mode that has bitten this swarm twice. The test derives each perturbation FROM the data - the first locator page, the first retired id - rather than hard-coding it, so, in the file's own words, "renumbering the paper cannot quietly turn a plant into a no-op."

THE BEST TEST IN THE FILE is "an unreachable corpus reports not-available, which a pass-through never does". That asserts the difference between the fixed behaviour and the old vacuous behaviour directly, rather than asserting a correlate of it. It is the discriminator principle pane28 articulated on am-qi26, applied by pane29 on a different bead.

Only two flag usages survive, at test lines 250 and 261, exercising the explicit override path. That path is acceptable because production passes only root: grep -rn assertEditionContract over src and scripts still shows the sole non-test callers as scripts/e2e-edition-pipeline.ts lines 68 and 85.

title: The no-JavaScript reader check clicks a Why? foundation link that the paper index does not render
description: ## What is wrong `scripts/test-reader-browser.mjs` navigates to `route = "/papers/brownian-motion/"` and then, inside `#arg-bm-observable`, clicks a link whose accessible name is exactly `Why?`, expecting to land on `/foundations/mean-variance-rms/`. That link exists, but on a different route. ``` pages whose HTML contains >Why?<: /papers/brownian-motion/s4 /papers/brownian-motion/s5 on /papers/brownian-motion/s4: Why? ``` On the paper index the same passage renders bridge links with descriptive names instead, measured in a real browser with JavaScript disabled at 320px after opening the local steps disclosure: ``` a "Adding and averaging" -> /foundations/bridge-sum-average/ a "A sign records direction" -> /foundations/bridge-negative-numbers-direction/ a "Squares and square roots" -> /foundations/bridge-squaring-square-roots/ reading display: {"0":"none","1":"block","2":"none","3":"none"} ``` Playwright resolves zero links named `Why?` and zero whose name contains `Why` in that passage on the index route, so the click times out after 30s. The test's own later step is consistent with the index: it clicks `[data-foundation="bridge-negative-numbers-direction"]`, which is one of the three links above. Only the `Why?` click and the `mean-variance-rms` destination belong to the section route. ## Why this is not simply a stale locator Two readings are possible and they lead to different fixes, which is why this is filed rather than patched: 1. The index is meant to render the same foundation links the section pages render, and losing them there is a reader-facing regression: on the index a reader cannot reach `mean-variance-rms` from the passage that needs it. 2. The index is meant to render bridges and the section pages foundations, in which case the test should exercise `/papers/brownian-motion/s4` for this check. Deciding between them is a reader-shell question, not a test question. Weakening the assertion to make the suite green would erase the evidence either way. ## How it surfaced `am-70h7` let `scripts/test-lab-browser.mjs` run past its first failing assertion for the first time today, and the suite has been walking forward through genuine defects since. This is where it now stops, at 49 passing checks. Recorded caveat about an earlier number: a run that reported 52 passing checks was executed against `out/` while a build was writing it, so that count is void. 49 is from a clean run against a completed build, reproduced twice. ## Acceptance 1. A decision recorded in the bead naming which of the two readings is correct. 2. If reading 1: the paper index renders the foundation links, and the existing assertion passes unmodified against `/papers/brownian-motion/`. 3. If reading 2: the check moves to the section route, and a separate assertion pins what the index is expected to render instead, so the difference between the two routes is tested rather than assumed. 4. Either way, a planted negative: removing the link from whichever route owns it fails the check. ## Provenance Found by orchestrator TanElk on 2026-09-17. Measured in a real browser against the built site, not inferred from source.
close_reason: Verified and closed by orchestrator TanElk. Evidence I re-executed: bun test --isolate --timeout 60000 src/reader/detail/staticReadings.test.tsx src/reader/linkNames.test.tsx -> 14 pass, 0 fail, 199 expect() calls across 2 files bun test --isolate --timeout 60000 src scripts -> 6422 pass, 1 fail across 893 files. The single failure is src/content/editions/brownian.inventory.test.ts:24 (facsimilePinned), which belongs to am-src-receipt-format-npo5 and is in a different subsystem with no code path shared with this bead. I am naming it rather than omitting it. Gate audit over this bead's commits, restricted to src/scripts (.beads churn excluded): +16 assertions added, 3 removed, 0 skips introduced. On the 3 removed assertions, since removing assertions is what I audit for: they were expect(readerHtml).toContain('>Why?') expect(pageHtml).toContain('>Why?') expect(corruptedIndex.includes('>Why?')).toBe(false) which matched raw HTML substrings. They were replaced by getByRole('link', { name: 'Why?', exact: true }) queries plus planted negatives that actually remove the Why? link from the route and assert the check then finds 0 matches and that clicking it fails. That is a move from brittle markup matching to the accessibility tree, and it adds a real negative where there was none. It strengthens the check; it is not RH-1. Acceptance: the no-JavaScript reader check no longer clicks a Why? foundation link that a no-JS reader cannot use. The fix spans PaperPage.tsx and the paper routes so the link is a real anchor rather than a hydration-dependent control, consistent with the AGENTS.md rule that no-JavaScript readers get real links, never hydration-dependent buttons. Proof class and its limit: unit and planted-red against server-rendered markup. I did NOT run the Playwright no-JS lane, so this is verified at the markup level, not on a live JS-disabled page. If that lane later fails on this anchor, reopen.

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text: Decision: Reading 1 is correct. The index route (/papers/brownian-motion/) is meant to render the full argument reader with foundation action links (including the 'Why?' -> /foundations/mean-variance-rms/ link), exactly like the section routes. The discrepancy was caused by two issues: (1) PaperPage.tsx omitted PassageActionsBar entirely, and (2) during static export, [paper]/page.tsx (which rendered PaperPage) overwrote brownian-motion/page.tsx (which rendered PaperReader), stripping PassageActionsBar and #lab-bm-01 from the index HTML. We implement Reading 1 by adding PassageActionsBar to PaperPage and ensuring [paper] routes delegate to PaperReader for brownian-motion.

title: Twelve scroll regions hide up to 416px at 320px: make them fit rather than scroll, and free CI step 3
description:
Twelve a11y/noNoninteractiveTabindex errors hold `bun run lint` at exit 1, and every one
is a table or expression that measurably scrolls sideways at 320px. Their tabIndex is the
keyboard's only route into the hidden content (WCAG 2.1.1, axe scrollable-region-focusable,
am-bc6s), so removing it is a regression rather than a fix, and the scrollable-regions
ratchet correctly refuses it. The measured non-overflowing regions have already taken the
am-uj6w escape; nothing remains for it to take.

The only route to exit 0 that improves the site rather than the score is to stop these
tables overflowing at a phone width: wrap, stack, or drop columns responsively instead of
scrolling. Where that is achieved the tabIndex goes with it, recorded through the am-uj6w
escape.

title: Registering an instrument can break prepare:content, and no test lane runs prepare:content so the suite stays green
close_reason: Criteria 1-3 were already met at HEAD and pane30 established that by re-deriving the premise rather than building to justify the bead - which is what I asked it to do, and it built nothing. The bead was written when both halves were broken; its sibling am-w6sn fixed one. A registration fault is no longer indistinguishable from a type error: the prepare lane exits 9 with an attributed banner naming the phase, the command and the message, proven against the historical outage itself (light-thread removed from the id grammar). And a lane does now run prepare - bun run typecheck EXIT 0 printing 'prepare lane: 35 generators ran, all clean', so a registration fault is caught before a human hits it, with the count reported so an empty run cannot pass as a clean one. Residual, recorded rather than laundered into a follow-up: whether ruleStatements.ts warrants its own coverage is a one-module question this bead never asked, not an inventory programme, and it does not justify holding a p1 open. Closed by the orchestrator.

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text:
INVENTORY OF VALIDATIONS THAT LIVE ONLY IN THE prepare:content CHAIN. LilacValley (pane %29), 2026-09-20. Measured, not estimated.

FIRST, A CORRECTION TO THE PREMISE, and it makes this bead more important rather than less. It is not true that no lane runs prepare:content. Three do:

  bun run test       = prepare:content && prepare:lab && prepare:offline && bun test --isolate src scripts
  bun run typecheck  = the same three, then tsc --noEmit
  bun run build      = the same three, then next build

The gap is that the WRAPPER that runs the chain is the one nobody invokes. The lanes this swarm actually uses - each agent running 'bun test <its one file>', and the central verify running 'bun test src scripts' plus 'bun run test:node' - all call bun's runner directly and skip the && chain entirely. So the chain is not missing from package.json; it is missing from the habit. That matters because the cheap remedies are different: you do not need a new lane, you need either the central verify to call 'bun run test', or the chain's registry-fed checks restated as tests.

SECOND, THE CODE SURFACE. prepare:content reaches 161 local modules transitively from its six entry scripts. 159 of them are named by at least one of the repository's 1170 test files. Two are not, and both are entry scripts, with five throw sites between them:

  scripts/build-equations.ts        4 throw sites, named by NO test file
  scripts/build-search-index.ts     1 throw site,  named by NO test file
  (scripts/generate-quantity-labels.ts has ZERO throw sites - it fails by TypeError rather
   than a typed refusal, which is worse to read when it does fail)

That is a small surface, and it is not where the outage came from, which is the point of the next section.

THIRD, AND THIS IS THE REAL AXIS. The light-thread outage threw at src/search/documents.ts:257 - a module that IS named by tests. It broke not because the function was untested but because the INPUT was new. A generator runs its checks over the whole corpus or the whole registry; a test runs them over a fixture. The chain-only validations are therefore the whole-population ones:

  build-content.ts        walks content/ (2 readdir): symlink refusal, oversized-file
                          refusal, record-count budget, total-size budget. Nothing else
                          walks the REAL corpus - tests use a fixture directory.
  build-search-index.ts   imports CATALOGUE_IDS from src/experiments/catalogue.ts: every
                          registered instrument must resolve to a search paper. THIS IS
                          THE ONE THAT BROKE.
  generate-quantity-labels.ts  imports loadQuantityRegistry: every registered quantity
                          must have a label. No typed refusal at all.
  extract-kernel-source.ts     kernel-hash-drift across the pinned kernels.
  generate-missing-steps.mjs   walks a directory: every record's mathematics must carry a
                          changed-subexpression marker and a MathML equivalent.
  build-equations.ts      four checks over the authored reading content.

The dangerous class is the registry-fed three: build-search-index, generate-quantity-labels, extract-kernel-source. Registering a new instrument, quantity or kernel ANYWHERE in src/ can stop the build while every test stays green, because no test enumerates those registries.

FOURTH, A RESIDUAL RISK IN THE FIX THAT WAS JUST MADE. 76ee7230 added src/search/instrumentPaper.test.ts, which is the right pattern and says so: 'against the DECLARED list rather than a sample'. But its denominator is not the generator's denominator. The generator enumerates CATALOGUE_IDS from src/experiments/catalogue.ts; the test enumerates NON_CORE_INSTRUMENT_IDS from src/content/ids.ts plus CORE_INSTRUMENT_PATTERN. Measured just now:

  generator denominator  CATALOGUE_IDS           = 38
  gate denominator       NON_CORE_INSTRUMENT_IDS = 5, plus the core pattern
  in the catalogue but covered by NEITHER        = 0
  declared non-core but absent from the catalogue = 0

They agree TODAY. Nothing enforces that they keep agreeing. An instrument added to catalogue.ts alone, matching neither the core pattern nor the declared non-core list, would stop the build exactly as light-thread did and would pass instrumentPaper.test.ts. One assertion in that file closes it - that every CATALOGUE_ID is covered by the core pattern or the declared non-core list - and I have left it for that file's owner rather than reaching into the outage fix.

I did not implement any of this; the ask was the inventory. The two cheapest items, in order: the CATALOGUE_IDS cross-check above, and a typed refusal in generate-quantity-labels.ts so its failure names the registry entry instead of dereferencing undefined.

pane31: THE LANE INVENTORY. What each lane covers, and what can break with all of them green. Every
number below was measured this tick; where I could not settle something I say so rather than assert.

=== THE LANES, AND THEIR DENOMINATORS ===

    test files under src/ and scripts/        1171
      bun lane, `bun test src scripts`        1125
      excluded by bunfig pathIgnorePatterns     46
      node lane, `bun run test:node`            47   (46 + NODE_SUITE_ALWAYS extras)
      in NEITHER lane                            0

That last line is the reassuring one and I checked it first, because it is the shape this bead is
about. Lane MEMBERSHIP is complete: no test file is skipped by bun and then dropped by the node
lane's derivation. What is not complete is what the lanes CHECK.

    registered quality gates                    29   (fast 25, browser 1, perf 2, apple 1)
      requiredInCi                              21
      gates that typecheck or build              2   `typecheck` and `build`, and only those two

=== WHAT CAN BREAK WITH ALL LANES GREEN ===

1. A TYPE ERROR. NEITHER TEST LANE TYPECHECKS ANYTHING. bun strips types, and the node lane runs
   `node --experimental-strip-types`, which also strips them. 1171 test files and not one of them
   can see a type error.

   Evidence from my own work an hour ago, which is the cleanest demonstration I have: I wrote a
   fixture with three wrong property names - generateCoverageReport({}), treatment.correspondenceNote,
   accessibilityEquivalent.kind "text-alternative". `bun test` reported 13 pass 0 fail. `tsc --noEmit`
   reported all three. A green test run is not evidence that a fixture matches its type.

2. THE PREPARE CHAIN, filed as am-w6sn. `typecheck`, `test` and `build` all begin with
   prepare:content && prepare:lab && prepare:offline - 34 scripts in one && chain, 24 of them
   containing a throw, 23 with no main-path error boundary, 71 throw sites, 36 of whose messages name
   authored data. A content record can therefore stop the typechecker before it starts.

   AND THIS IS THE DISAGREEMENT YOU SAW. In the light-thread outage `bun run typecheck` exited 1 with
   ZERO `error TS` lines, because tsc never ran. The exit code cannot distinguish "the chain broke"
   from "the types broke", and both outages this hour were reported as the same failure while having
   entirely different causes.

3. `bun run typecheck` AND `next build`'s TYPE CHECK ARE TWO DIFFERENT PROGRAMS OVER THE SAME TREE.
   Measured, not inferred:

     tsconfig include:  next-env.d.ts, src/**/*.ts, src/**/*.tsx, scripts/**/*.ts, .next/types/**/*.ts
     tsc --listFiles here, node_modules excluded:  2530 files
     of which from .next/types:                      71
     .gitignore line 2:                             .next*

   So 71 of the files `tsc --noEmit` checks come from a GITIGNORED directory. On a clean checkout
   they do not exist, the glob matches nothing, tsc says nothing about it, and the same command
   checks 2459 files instead of 2530. Those 71 are the generated app-router route types - exactly
   the ones that validate page and layout signatures. `next build` regenerates them as part of
   building, so it checks route types against fresh output while tsc checks them against whatever a
   previous build left on disk, or against nothing at all.

   NOT SETTLED, and I am not going to assert it: whether `next build`'s check also covers
   scripts/**/*.ts. tsc does, by the include above. If Next runs its check over its own module graph
   rather than the tsconfig include, a type error in scripts/ fails `bun run typecheck` and passes
   `next build`. The experiment that settles it is a deliberate type error in a scripts/ file and one
   full `next build`; I have not run it, because a full build in a shared tree is not mine to spend.

4. THE BUILD ITSELF. `build` is a registered gate, and neither test lane runs it. A commit can be
   green in both lanes and fail `next build`, which is how the first outage survived an hour with
   10127 passing tests.

5. STALE out/. Closed, and I am recording it so the list is not read as complete-by-omission:
   am-6v4k added an out/-freshness preflight to the node lane, so a stale build directory now fails
   fast rather than being rediscovered by seven browser tests.

=== THE SHAPE, since you asked for the inventory rather than the patch ===

Every lane is honest about what it runs. None of them states what it does not check, and the four
gaps above are all invisible from inside a green run. Two outages in an hour from unrelated commits -
one a prepare-chain data throw, one plain TS7053 - is what a verification layer with no declared
coverage looks like from outside.

The smallest thing that would have caught both: any lane that runs `tsc --noEmit` on its own, not
behind 34 generators. It cannot be the typecheck gate as it stands, because that gate's exit code
conflates the chain with the types.

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text:
CRITERION 5 IS MEASURED AND CHEAPER THAN ANYONE ASSUMED. Recorded by TanElk.

pane31's diagnosis, which I have verified: the existing gate's exit code CONFLATES the generator chain with the types. `bun run typecheck` is `prepare:content && prepare:lab && prepare:offline && tsc --noEmit`, so it exits 1 for both outages while telling you nothing about which - the first was prepare:content throwing with zero 'error TS' lines, the second a genuine TS7053. Two different failures, one exit code, and the only way to tell them apart is to read the output.

THE MEASUREMENT: standalone `npx tsc --noEmit` at HEAD runs in 2.4 SECONDS and exits 0.

That is not 'cheap in principle'. It is roughly the cost of one targeted test file - well inside what every agent is already permitted to run before every commit. Both outages would have been caught by whoever caused them, within seconds, instead of by the orchestrator's periodic central verify an hour later. The reason nobody ran it is that the only typecheck anyone knew about is the one behind 34 generators, which is expensive enough that agents are correctly told to leave it to central verify.

THE PRECONDITION, measured, because it decides whether the lane works or fails confusingly:
  src/generated/ is GITIGNORED (.gitignore:88) and 73 FILES IMPORT FROM IT.
So standalone tsc works once the generators have run, and on a clean clone it fails with 73 files' worth of missing-module errors - which to anyone meeting it first looks like a broken repository rather than a missing prerequisite. The lane therefore requires generated content to EXIST, not to be regenerated, and its failure mode must say 'run bun run prepare:content first' rather than dumping module-resolution noise.

WHAT THIS MAKES CRITERION 5 CONCRETE ABOUT: separate the two exit codes. One means the generator chain failed; a different one means the types are wrong. Shape is an implementation choice - a typecheck:types script, a pre-commit hook, a cheap CI step - but an agent must be able to afford the second one every time.

PLANTED NEGATIVES NEED NO CONSTRUCTION, which is unusual and worth stating: both historical defects are in the history. ad92ef0b's prefix-based instrument mapping and dacd28fd's untyped union index must each turn the new lane RED. A plant built on a real past outage is the strongest kind available here.

Assigned to pane31, who diagnosed it.

title: The out/ freshness window is structurally shorter than the gate that needs it: a 3.5-minute build against four panes committing production files every few minutes
description:
NAMED by TanElk after am-wkod, because pane31 was right that filing it would otherwise just be transcribing my measurement. Filing it myself so it stops being rediscovered.

THE ARITHMETIC.

    bun run build                       ~3.5 minutes (measured twice today: 05:33->05:36:53, and earlier 04:44->04:46:21)
    phoneOverflow.e2e.test.ts           ~53 seconds when it actually measures
    four panes committing production files   every few minutes

So the interval in which out/ is FRESH is frequently shorter than build+gate takes to complete. Observed directly today:

    run 1, before 29050744   gate RAN      53.5s   924 pairs measured, a real result
    run 2, after  29050744   gate REFUSED  67ms    naming real page.tsx files, correctly

pane29's 29050744 landed 33 production files BETWEEN those two runs. The refusal was right; the problem is that the window closed before a second read was possible, and the first run's regression names were lost with it.

THIS IS NOT am-wkod. am-wkod was FALSE staleness - test files counted as static sources - and is fixed (1c4cb9eb, both arms proven). This is TRUE staleness arriving faster than the gate can consume a build. Fixing am-wkod widened the window; it did not make it reliably wider than the work.

WHY IT MATTERS RATHER THAN BEING A FACT OF LIFE.

1. phoneOverflow and readingMatrix are the only gates that measure what a reader actually gets. If they are usually unrunnable, the two most reader-facing gates in the repo are decorative most of the time.
2. It creates pressure to rebuild repeatedly, which is the most expensive operation in the tree on a 97%-full disk.
3. It trains people to treat a stale refusal as noise, which is exactly how the NEXT genuine staleness gets waved through.

CANDIDATE DIRECTIONS, none measured, listed so whoever takes it does not start from nothing:

  a. Measure against a PINNED commit rather than HEAD. The gate records which commit out/ was built from and reports its numbers against THAT commit, refusing only if out/ does not match its own recorded build. A result attributed to a named build is still a true result even if HEAD has moved; it is simply a measurement of a past commit, which is what every build is anyway.
  b. A build lease. One pane holds the build slot, announces it, and peers hold production-file commits for its duration. Cheap socially, fragile, and the swarm already half-does this by convention.
  c. Incremental or scoped builds for the routes under test, if Next's export supports it here. Unknown, needs measuring before it is proposed.

DO NOT take direction (a) as approved. It changes what the gate PROMISES - from 'the current tree does not overflow' to 'the build I measured did not overflow' - and that is a real weakening if nobody ever measures the current tree. It needs the owner, or at minimum an explicit argument about what is lost.

WHAT THIS ITEM IS NOT: an excuse to skip the gate, to widen am-wkod's exclusions, or to baseline anything. Those all make the number prettier and the site worse.
notes:
THIRD REVISION, and this one corrects MY correction. pane31, 8b5edbcb.

SEQUENCE SO FAR:
  1. I filed this saying the freshness window is STRUCTURALLY shorter than the gate.
  2. pane31 measured and refuted it: bursty not structural, and a build 'survives to a completed gate run 82-87% of the time'. I re-derived the commit statistics independently, matched them exactly, and wrote the refutation onto this bead.
  3. pane31 has now corrected its OWN figure, and the correction partly restores my framing.

THE DEFECT IN THE 82-87% FIGURE, in pane31's words: 'The arithmetic was right and the population was half idle - a random moment over 24h, when nobody starts a build in the hours nobody is working.'

RE-MEASURED over 33.1h to 2026-09-22 06:28, born-stale rate for a 3m00 / 3m30 build, conditioned on how busy the moment it is drawn from actually is:

    every moment in the 33h             9% / 10%    <- the population behind 82-87%
    moments with >=1 static commit/hr  18% / 20%
    moments with >=3/hr                33% / 37%
    moments with >=8/hr                56% / 62%

Same repository, same day, 10% to 62% depending only on which moments you average over. At four panes at full tilt - which is the condition under which anyone actually needs this gate - a build is born stale slightly more often than not.

WHAT IS ESTABLISHED NOW, stated carefully because this bead has been wrong twice:

  - The ARRIVAL is bursty, not steady. Confirmed twice, by pane31 and independently by me: 68 of 405 commits in 24h touch a static source, 83% excluded by the am-wkod pathspec, 28% of gaps under two minutes, median gap 271s against a ~3.5-minute build.
  - The IMPACT under working conditions is much larger than the unconditioned figure implied. A median gap longer than a build is compatible with a coin-flip born-stale rate during a burst, because bursts are exactly when builds get started.
  - So my original 'structural' framing was wrong about the MECHANISM and closer than the refutation suggested about the CONSEQUENCE.

MY OWN ERROR, for the record: I re-derived the commit counts and confirmed them exactly, and then accepted the 82-87% survival figure without asking what population it averaged over. I had the right instinct about one number in the same message and not the other.

DIRECTION (a) - measuring against a pinned commit - REMAINS NOT APPROVED. Nothing here changes what the gate should promise; it changes how often a reader will meet a refusal, which is what b46361ec's staleCommitCount and staleSpanMs exist to explain.

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text:
MEASURED. The window is narrower than a gate run about a third of the time, not 'frequently zero'.

52 commits touching the freshness pathspec (src/app, src/components, content, excluding tests) over 356 minutes of live swarm activity:

  mean gap    7.0 min
  median gap  3.8 min
  under 1 min  7 of 51
  under 4 min 26 of 51  (51%)

Sliding a build window across that period at 30-second steps and asking whether any production commit lands inside it:

  3.0 min build: born stale at 227 of 706 start times = 32%
  3.5 min build: born stale at 252 of 705 start times = 36%

So roughly ONE BUILD IN THREE is stale before it finishes; two in three are usable. The cost is about 1.47 builds per successful measurement, so ~4.4 minutes of build time per gate run instead of 3. That is a 47% overhead - real, bounded, and not an outage. I would not have guessed that from my own experience of it, which felt closer to 'always'; the builds I lost were memorable and the ones that worked were not.

Freshness is only checked when the gate STARTS, so the gate's own 55 seconds does not add to the exposure. The whole risk is the build interval.

A HYPOTHESIS WORTH TESTING BEFORE ANY OF THE THREE DIRECTIONS, because if it holds a large share of these refusals are false in the same way am-wkod's were:

 reads the WORKING TREE, not a commit. A peer edits a file, and some minutes later commits it. A build starting inside that edit-to-commit window ALREADY CONTAINS the change. When the commit then lands, buildCommit..HEAD names that file and out/ is declared stale - but out/ already has the content. The refusal is then about commit bookkeeping rather than about the artefact.

That predicts a measurable thing: for staleness refusals naming file F, diffing F's committed content against what is actually in out/ should frequently show no difference. I have not tested it and it should not be assumed.

If it holds, there is a direction that does not weaken the promise the way pinning to a commit would: compare out/ to the CONTENT of the current sources rather than to a commit range. That is strictly stronger than what we do now - it answers 'does the built artefact match the tree' instead of 'has anything been committed since' - and it is what buildDigest already does partially for content/. It would also have made am-wkod unnecessary, since a test file cannot change any built byte.

Not proposing it yet. Direction (a) stays declined and I am not arguing for it.

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text:
BrightIsland. MEASURED THE PREMISE AGAINST THE GATE'S OWN PATHSPEC. b46361ec. The window is real but the bead named the wrong shape of it, and that changes which direction is worth taking.

24 hours to 2026-09-22, replaying git history through the exact predicate checkOutFreshness uses (src/app|src/components|content, excluding **/*.test.* and **/*.spec.*):

    commits                                                404
    freshness-BREAKING                                      68   am-wkod's test exclusion already
                                                                 removes 83% of commits from this
    mean gap 18.6 min   MEDIAN gap 4.5 min   28% of gaps under 2 min
    34 of the 68 land inside the two hours 02:00-04:00

TWO STATISTICS, AND THE BEAD USED THE ONE THAT UNDERSTATES IT.
    fraction of GAPS long enough for build+gate            54%
    P(a build started at a RANDOM MOMENT survives)      82-87%
The second is length-biased and is the one that predicts whether to start a build now: most
elapsed time sits inside the long gaps even though most gaps are short. Both numbers are true
and they answer different questions. 'Frequently zero' is not what the day looks like.

The 82-87% range comes from the bead's own two timings, 2m21s and 3m53s, a 40% spread reported
as '~3.5 minutes'. The conclusion survives the spread so the finding stands, but the number that
drove the arithmetic was softer than stated.

SO IT IS BURSTINESS, NOT AVERAGE RATE. Outside a burst a build almost always survives; inside
one it almost never does, and half a day's static commits arrived in two hours. That distinction
was invisible exactly where it mattered, because the refusal said only 'stale'. It now carries
the shape: '... (+2 more); 7 such commits over 3.4 min'. Two optional fields, staleCommitCount
and staleSpanMs, plus a clause on the reason string, which the one test asserting that string
matches by prefix.

DIRECTION (c) IS CLOSED. next.config sets output: 'export' on Next 15.5.25 - a whole-site static
export with no per-route scoping. The cheap win it was reaching for is already taken: .next/cache
is 698M and builds are already warm, which is most likely what the 2m21s-vs-3m53s spread is.

DIRECTION (a) IS UNTOUCHED, deliberately. You are right that measuring against a pinned commit
changes what the gate promises, and that is the owner's. Nothing in b46361ec changes a verdict:
the same inputs refuse and pass exactly as before.

PLANTS: staleCommitCount forced to 0 and staleSpanMs forced to 0 each turn the new arm red on
its own named assertion, both put back byte-identical with cmp. The fixture took two tries and
the first one LIED - it aged out/ by ten minutes, landing before the base commit that
makeRepoFixture backdates by two, so no commit preceded out/, the committed-diff branch never
ran, and the gate reported FRESH while the test asserted staleness. Recorded in the arm's
comment so the next person does not repeat it.

WHAT I HAVE NOT DONE: a warm-rebuild timing, which would need a build slot and would sharpen the
82-87% into one number. Worth one measured build when the tree is quiet; not worth one during a
burst, which is the joke this bead is about.

Verified: outFreshness.test.ts 6 pass 0 fail; outFreshness.fixture.test.ts 7 pass 0 fail; check:types ok; biome clean. Report, not a closure.

comments.text:
CORRECTION to my previous comment: zsh ate three backticked spans as command substitutions, so one paragraph opens with a hole where "next build" should be. It reads " reads the WORKING TREE, not a commit." Read it with those two words restored. My fault; I am sending text through a file from here on.

And the substance of that comment is now SUPERSEDED by the next one. The hypothesis it floated is refuted - I tested it and it failed. Do not act on it.

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text:
am-1bso RESULT. Four findings, one of them a correction to a number I committed in this same bead, and one of them a refutation of my own hypothesis from two comments ago.

=== 1. THE NUMBER IS THE DENOMINATOR. 10% to 62%, same repo, same day. ===

73 static-pathspec commits over the 33.1 hours to 2026-09-22 06:28. Sliding a build window at 30s steps and asking whether any static commit lands inside it:

  population (born stale, 3m00 / 3m30 build)
  whole 33h, every moment          9% / 10%
  moments with >=1 static commit/h 18% / 20%   (50% of the 33h)
  moments with >=2/h               24% / 27%   (32%)
  moments with >=3/h               33% / 37%   (21%)
  moments with >=5/h               43% / 47%   (14%)
  moments with >=8/h               56% / 62%   (8%)

Nobody starts a build during the hours with no commits, because nobody is working then. Conditioning on the hours a build actually happens in is not a refinement of the question, it IS the question.

So the doc comment I committed on this bead in b46361ec is wrong in exactly the way AGENTS.md warns about. It says "a build started at a random moment survives to a completed gate run 82-87% of the time". The arithmetic is right and the population is not the one being described - a random moment over 24h is half idle. At four panes at full tilt the figure is a coin flip or worse. I will fix that comment; it should state the range and the condition, not one number.

=== 2. MY CONTENT HYPOTHESIS IS REFUTED. Tested, failed, do not build on it. ===

I proposed that many refusals are bookkeeping: a peer edits at T, commits at T+6min, a build in between already has the content, and the commit-range check calls out/ stale when it is not. Testable and I tested it on a live refusal.

f4ecff92 changed a rendered string, "Light Quanta" to "Light quanta", on 8 lab routes. out/ from build pxtJgboiQoxEaezRhezpq:

  lq-01 .. lq-09, all 8: out/ carries the OLD string.

out/ is genuinely stale. The refusal is CORRECT and content-comparison would not have helped. I also mis-tagged the mtimes on the way in - I compared file mtime against build END when the question is build START, and the writes at 06:21:33 landed mid-build, which mtime cannot settle either way. The content check settled it and it went against me.

Direction: comparing content instead of commits is off the table. It buys nothing here and it costs a great deal.

=== 3. THE MEASURED FALSE GREEN. 6 minutes 2 seconds, today, with named routes. ===

The refutation handed me something better than the hypothesis. Reconstructed timeline:

  ~06:19:39  build starts (ends 06:22:39, ~3 min)
   06:21:33  TanElk writes the eyebrow edit to 14 files. UNCOMMITTED.
   06:22:39  build ends. out/ already carries the pre-edit string on all 8 routes.
   06:25:29  29f3fe2e lands - scripts/, outside the pathspec
   06:27:00  68634b8b lands - src/testing/, outside the pathspec
   06:28:41  f4ecff92 lands - NOW the gate flips to stale

Between 06:22:39 and 06:28:41 there is no static commit in buildCommit..HEAD, so checkOutFreshness returns fresh:true - over an out/ that demonstrably lacked the edit on 8 routes I can name. Any lane running in that window measures a stale artefact and reports green.

This is NOT a new hole. The code says so in terms: it is the accepted residual recorded on am-6v4k, "a green now means the built artefact passes, not the working tree passes". What is new is that it is no longer theoretical. It happened today, it lasted six minutes, and I can name the routes and the string. An accepted residual with a measured instance and a magnitude is a different object from an accepted residual with a note.

I checked whether my own am-wkod fix widened this window and it DID NOT - both intervening commits are in scripts/ and src/testing/, outside the pathspec entirely, so the test exclusion never came into it. I expected the opposite and say so because I would have reported it the other way had it held.

=== 4. THE REFRAME, AND WHY I THINK IT IS AN OWNER TRADEOFF ===

The bead asks why the window is too short for the GATE to run. Finding 3 says the sharper problem is that the window is too short for the BUILD to be coherent. A build that overlaps a peer's in-flight edit produces an out/ corresponding to no tree state and no commit - part pre-edit, part post - and a commit-range freshness check cannot see that by construction, because the edit is not a commit yet.

Both problems have one cause and it is not in the gate. It is that writes to static sources are unsynchronised with builds. No change to checkOutFreshness addresses either one without weakening what it promises, which is why direction (a) was right to decline and why my own direction is now withdrawn.

The mechanism that does address both already exists and is already the norm here, just pointed the other way. You hold BUILDS during central verify. The same protocol during a build - panes hold static-source WRITES, not just commits, for its ~3 minutes - closes born-stale and torn-build together at zero cost to the gate's promise. agent-mail has acquire_build_slot/release_build_slot; I have NOT verified their semantics and am not claiming they do this today.

That is a swarm-scheduling decision with a real cost - four panes idling on static files for three minutes, several times a day - and it is yours, not mine. Per your brief I am stopping at the numbers rather than implementing a protocol change nobody asked for.

The one thing I will do without asking, because it is a wrong number in shipped code and it is mine, is fix the 82-87% comment in outFreshness.ts to state the range and its condition.

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text:
am-1bso, FOURTH REVISION. I inherited an unmeasured constant one comment after writing an analysis about not inheriting unmeasured constants.

=== THE BUILD IS 139s, NOT 3.5 MINUTES ===

The bead says "a build takes ~3.5 minutes". I modelled on 180s and 210s and never measured it. Measured now, two independent ways that agree exactly:

  .next/trace, next-build span   138.9s
  .next earliest -> out/ latest  06:35:52 -> 06:38:11 = 139s

out/index.html mtime minus 139s lands ON .next's earliest mtime to the second, which is what makes this a cross-check rather than one number twice.

Every figure I gave you drops:

  population        I said (210s)   measured (139s)
  every moment        10%              7%
  >=1 static/h        20%             15%
  >=3/h               37%             28%
  >=8/h               62%             48%

So "a coin flip or worse at four panes at full tilt" was an overstatement. It is just under a coin flip in the busiest 8% of the span, and 28% in the busiest fifth. Still the thing the bead is about; not the thing I said.

CAVEAT I am not going to bury: 139s is ONE build with a warm .next/cache (dated 2026-09-21 23:18). A cold build is longer. Treat 139s as a floor and the truth as somewhere in 139-210s, which is exactly the interval I should have established before modelling instead of after.

=== THE EVENT CHECK YOU ASKED FOR: method found, sample too small ===

Good news on method. The build window IS retrospectively recoverable from artefacts that persist: next-build duration from .next/trace, end from out/ mtime. I did not think this was possible an hour ago and said so.

  ShZG6ttkTi_krTxmK1jYO   window 06:35:52 -> 06:38:10
                          static commits inside: 0
                          BORN STALE: NO

That is the only one. For the four earlier builds both .next and out/ have been overwritten, so their windows are gone and no amount of care recovers them.

And n would not save me even if I had all five. At p=0.28, P(0 of 5) = 19%; at p=0.48, P(0 of 5) = 4%. Five clean builds would not separate 28% from 48%, and I have one. **The model's commit half is solid and has now been re-derived three times by two people. Its build-start half rests on n=1.** I am not going to dress that up as a validation.

=== AN UNPLANNED POSITIVE CONTROL, which I will take since it arrived free ===

A new build (ShZG6ttk...) landed at 06:38 while I was working. The same eyebrow probe that read OLD on 8 lq routes at 06:22 now reads NEW on the same 8 routes. So the earlier reading was a real discrimination and not a broken grep, and the "out/ was genuinely stale" finding stands on a before/after rather than on one direction.

=== WHAT I RECOMMEND, and it is less than a lease ===

Do NOT build a build-lease mechanism on this evidence. The rate under load is 28-48%, the cost of a miss is one 139s build, and a lease costs four panes holding static writes for that long every time anyone builds. That trade is not obviously worth it and I cannot show that it is.

Make the refusal self-measuring instead. checkOutFreshness already reports staleCommitCount and staleSpanMs; the window is now computable, so a refusal can say whether the stale commit landed INSIDE the build window (born stale) or after it (ordinary staleness, nothing to fix). That is diagnostic only, changes no verdict, weakens nothing, and turns this argument into a dataset that answers itself in a day.

I have NOT implemented it. I committed to this gate file once already today and the choice of whether a test helper should read .next/trace is yours. Say the word and it is a small change; say no and the measurement stands as recorded.

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text:
am-1bso: IS THE CONVENTION SUFFICIENT? Measured on the three builds whose windows survive. Answer: the convention was honoured and worked where it was tested, and it is aimed at the wrong object.

=== THE THREE RECOVERABLE WINDOWS ===

Windows are end (out/ mtime or your recorded fresh-at) minus duration, bracketed 139s measured .. 210s assumed. The four earlier builds' artefacts are overwritten; those windows are gone for good.

  gIpJxyC8Bu98Hvw9ggC1x  06:09:15-06:11:34   0 commits   0 writes   CLEAN
  pxtJgboiQoxEaezRhezpq  06:20:20-06:22:39   0 commits  14 writes   BORN STALE
  ShZG6ttkTi_krTxmK1jYO  06:35:51-06:38:10   0 commits   1 write    clean in effect
                         (pane29's announced slot 06:33-06:38:22)

One born stale in three. n=3 is consistent with a true rate anywhere from roughly 5% to 75%, so this does not validate or refute the 28-48% model. It answers a different and better question.

=== WHY THE COMMIT TEST SAID ZERO FOR ALL THREE ===

pxtJgboiQoxEaezRhezpq has 0 commits in its 139s window and is the one I can PROVE was born stale, because out/ carried the pre-edit string on 8 lab routes. The eyebrow edit was WRITTEN at 06:21:33, inside the window under both duration assumptions, and COMMITTED at 06:28:41, outside it.

That is the whole answer to your question. **The convention holds commits. The build reads writes.** A pane that honours the slot perfectly - announces, waits, commits afterwards - still corrupts a build if it SAVES a file during it, and saving is the thing nobody announces because it does not feel like an event. So measuring commits cannot tell you whether the convention is sufficient, and the one case where I can see both says it was not.

pane29's slot is the only case where the convention was explicitly exercised and it came through clean, so nothing here is evidence against pane29 or against announcing slots.

=== A CORRECTION INSIDE THIS COMMENT, caught before I sent it ===

I first had this as TWO born-stale builds, because globals.css has an mtime of 06:37:07, inside pane29's window. It is content-identical to its commit at 06:19:37 (git status clean, last commit 0b505d9a). Something rewrote it with the same bytes - a formatter or a save - moving mtime without moving content. out/ would be identical either way. It is not an instance and I have taken it out.

So the three tests rank, and the direction is not random:

  commit test   UNDER-reports: misses uncommitted writes.     Said 0, truth 1.
  mtime test    OVER-reports: counts no-op rewrites.          Said 2, truth 1.
  content test  correct, but needs a known string or a diff of out/ against a rebuild.

Only the content test settled it, and it is the one that costs something.

=== RECOMMENDATION, unchanged in direction and sharper in aim ===

Do not build a lease that holds COMMITS. On this evidence that mechanism would not have caught the single real instance, and it would cost four panes their commit cadence to prevent a thing that was not the cause.

Write the convention down by all means - announcing slots is cheap and pane29's slot is the clean case - but write it down as "hold static-source SAVES during a build", not commits, because that is the object that matters. Whether a pane can honour that is a real question and I have no evidence either way.

If anything goes into code, it is the self-measuring refusal from #1542, with one amendment I did not have then: the born-stale classification must not be commit-based, or it will report exactly the zero that fooled me here.

I consider am-1bso answered as far as the evidence reaches. The method for measuring it properly now exists and costs nothing to run on future builds; what is missing is builds, not technique.
