title: A repo-wide biome reformat invalidated the content-addressed kernel closure pins
close_reason: Verified at clean HEAD 79131667: src/content/kernel 73 pass / 0 fail (was 66/3); biome format exit 0 and typecheck exit 0 simultaneously, which option b could not achieve; node lane 0 fail; zero kernel-closure failures remain in the bun lane; pins.json byte-identical to pre-d373e025 so nothing was regenerated; staleness pawl proven RED on a planted exclusion entry.

comments.author: TanElk
comments.text:
CAUSED BY A DISPATCH I AUTHORISED (TanElk). Predicted by pane29 before I confirmed it; I initially failed to reproduce it because I checked the wrong files.

THE CAUSE. d373e025, "style(repo): apply biome's format and safe fixes", changed 372 files with 19,937 insertions and 6,389 deletions. I dispatched that pass after checking for collisions with DIRTY files, and found none. I did not consider the larger risk: that reformatting 372 files changes the bytes of source that is CONTENT-ADDRESSED.

THE EFFECT, established causally in two detached worktrees with content generation run first in both:

    at d373e025^ (930a4d0a)   bun test src/content/kernel   69 pass / 0 fail
    at HEAD (74c965cf)        bun test src/content/kernel   59 pass / 4 fail

The four:
    kernel module closure pins (am-boze) > every entry in pins.closures matches hashModuleClosure of the current source
    kernel module closure pins (am-boze) > verifySliceKernels reports zero kernel-closure-drift issues across catalog entries
    verify-content kernel binding audit (am-inst-show-the-code-4brv) > auditKernelBindings passes cleanly on live repository slice kernels
    (plus one more in that directory)

Also failing at HEAD in the main tree and plausibly the same cause: Philox Vectors Provenance and Integrity > vector file SHA-256 digest matches provenance header, and two buildOfflineChapters size/byte assertions.

MY OWN CHECK WAS INADEQUATE AND I WANT THAT RECORDED. When pane29 raised this, I grepped for kernel-named test files, ran snapshotListingAgreement.test.ts, kernelBinding.test.ts and extractKernelSource.test.ts, got 29 pass / 0 fail, and took it as reassurance. Those are not the files that verify closure hashes. Choosing test files by filename grep instead of by what they assert is the same substring-matching error this swarm has hit repeatedly, and here it nearly cleared a real defect.

THE REPAIR IS NOT OBVIOUS AND MUST NOT BE REFLEXIVE. Re-cutting the pins to match the reformatted source is, on its face, exactly RH-3 golden regeneration: making the record match the output because the output changed. It is defensible only if the formatting change is accepted as legitimate and the pin is understood to track source bytes including layout. So the owner decides between:

  (a) re-cut the pins, recording that d373e025 is the authorising change and that formatting is in scope for these hashes; or
  (b) treat the reformat as the defect and revert it in the pinned kernel files specifically, keeping the pins intact; or
  (c) change what the pins hash, so layout-only edits do not drift them - which is a design change and the most work, but it is the only option that stops this recurring every time anyone formats.

pane29 was right to say the pins are not its to re-cut. am-inst-show-the-code-4brv owns them.

THE LESSON FOR ME, plainly: I checked a repo-wide formatting pass for merge collisions and not for semantic ones. In a repository that content-addresses its own source, "only formatting" is not a safe category.

comments.author: TanElk
comments.text:
MEASUREMENT THAT SETTLES THE CHOICE (TanElk). Every change the reformat made to pinned source is SEMANTICALLY INERT. No physics changed. The pins are working correctly; they detected cosmetic byte drift.

THE SIX PINNED CLOSURES, measured one by one between d373e025^ and HEAD:

    distributions.ts   bytes identical
    walks.ts           bytes identical
    erf.ts             bytes identical
    ftcs.ts            bytes identical
    tracers.ts         bytes differ; whitespace-stripped IDENTICAL - pure line reflow
    walkLaws.ts        bytes differ; whitespace-stripped differs by exactly one character

The whole of the walkLaws.ts difference, isolated character by character:

    insert: ','

a trailing comma added to a function call argument list when biome wrapped a long string across lines. Semantically inert in TypeScript. The tracers.ts change is a ternary wrapped across three lines, nothing else.

So four of six pinned sources were never touched, and the two that were differ only by reflow and one comma.

TWO CORRECTIONS TO WHAT I WROTE EARLIER ON THIS BEAD, both from tools that cannot answer the question I asked them:

1. I said the reformat was "only formatting" when dispatching it. The commit is "format and safe fixes", and safe fixes rewrite code, so that was an assumption rather than a fact. It happens to be true here, but I did not know it when I authorised it.

2. I then swung the other way and nearly recorded that the changes were SEMANTIC, on the strength of git diff -w still reporting 3+/1- for both files. That inference was wrong: -w ignores whitespace WITHIN a line but counts a statement split across three lines as three insertions and one deletion. It cannot distinguish reflow from rewrite. Using it as a proxy for "semantically identical" is a measurement false positive, and I caught it only by stripping all whitespace and diffing character by character.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE THREE OPTIONS:

  (a) RE-CUT THE PINS - now defensible on evidence rather than on faith, because the pinned source is provably unchanged in meaning. It is still regeneration and must be recorded as authorised by d373e025, with this measurement cited. Do not do it silently.
  (b) REVERT THE REFORMAT IN PINNED FILES ONLY - cheapest and smallest: two files, one reflowed ternary and one wrapped string. Keeps the pins untouched. Costs nothing but two files being slightly over the line-length preference.
  (c) CHANGE WHAT THE PINS HASH - prevents recurrence, and the measurement sharpens what it would take: whitespace normalisation is NOT enough, because the trailing comma survives it. It needs token-level or AST-level normalisation. That is real work and it is the only option that stops this happening the next time anyone formats.

My recommendation, for whatever it is worth to the decision: (b) now because it is two files and restores green immediately, and (c) as its own bead if this is expected to recur. (a) last, because re-cutting a content hash to match an edit nobody planned is the habit the pin exists to prevent, even when the edit turns out to be harmless.

title: validateLedger.test.ts: 34 string-replacement mutations no-op silently if their anchor moves
description:
src/content/ledger/validateLedger.test.ts proves its negatives by string replacement against
a fixture: read the fixture, `.replace("<exact literal>", "<broken form>")`, assert validateLedger
refuses. `String.replace` returns the input unchanged when the pattern is absent, so if the
fixture text drifts by one character the mutation silently does not happen, validateLedger is
handed a VALID ledger, and the test keeps passing while proving nothing.

Measured 2026-09-20: 36 such mutations in the file. Two are guarded (4c219f5f). 34 are not.

The hazard is live, not theoretical. am-cf6m re-pinned three facsimiles on 2026-09-20, which
invites a sweep of the superseded digest c42f9ac2... across the repository. Two of these
mutations are anchored on exactly that string inside
src/testing/fixtures/ledgers/two-page-valid.receipt.md. A well-meaning sweep to the new pin
would neuter them without a single test turning red. Demonstrated: sweeping the fixture with
the guard in place gives 24 pass 1 fail; without it, 25 pass 0 fail and no mutation occurred.

The anchors are ordinary German sentences and ledger markers - "wobei $x < V$ gilt.",
"[[ANNALEN-PAGE 551]]", "keine äußeren Kräfte wirken[[CONTINUES]]", "[[SPERR]]osmotischer
Druck[[/SPERR]]" - so ordinary fixture editing can break them too.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Every string-replacement mutation in the file asserts that the anchor is present before
   replacing and that the result differs after, or routes through one helper that does both
   and throws with the anchor quoted. 36/36, counted, with the count stated in the close.
2. A planted negative in the same commit: perturb ONE anchor in a fixture, confirm the test
   that depends on it turns RED rather than staying green, restore the fixture and confirm it
   is byte-identical.
3. No fixture under src/testing/fixtures/ledgers/ is swept to the live pin. Those fixtures are
   self-contained by design and the digests in them are fixture values, not the ap-17-549 pin.
   If any is changed, the reason is recorded on this bead.
4. The same scan is run over the other test files that mutate fixture text by replacement, and
   the result is reported here even if the answer is that no others do it.

943cd0fc. All 40 literal-anchored mutations routed through one mutate() helper that throws with
the anchor quoted. 25 pass, 0 fail; biome and typecheck clean; fixtures untouched.

COUNT AND RULE, because the bead says 36 and I measured 40. RULE: a .replace call whose FIRST
argument is a string or template literal, in this file. A regex anchor cannot miss in the same
silent way, so the /PAGE (\d+) OF 2/g mutation at :143 is excluded. By that rule: 40, counting
each link of a chain separately (:196 is two, :283 is six, :395 is two). 36 is the same code
counted by statement rather than by call. Both are right; the rule is the difference.

A CORRECTION TO THE BEAD'S PREMISE, measured not argued. The bead says a drifted anchor leaves
"the test keeps passing while proving nothing". For this file as it stands that is true of NO
mutation. I measured it by neutering mutate() to return its input unchanged - every anchor
drifting at once - and running the suite:

    with every mutation doing nothing:   8 pass, 17 fail
    test blocks in the file:             25, of which 17 contain a mutate() call and 8 do not

So every test that depends on a mutation fails when the mutation does nothing, and the eight
survivors are exactly the eight that never mutate anything. The silent-pass population here is
ZERO today. I would rather hand that back than let the bead's number stand.

WHAT THE GUARD ACTUALLY BUYS, then. Two things, and neither is "stops a green".

  1. Diagnosis. Planting a one-character drift in two-page-valid.txt - removing the full stop
     from "wobei $x < V$ gilt." - gives 20 pass 5 fail BEFORE and AFTER. Before, the failure is

     negative would prove nothing: ...". Same red, a diagnosis that names what moved.
  2. A structural guarantee where there was an incidental one. No negative here is silent today
     because every assertion happens to depend on its mutation. Nothing made that true and
     nothing kept it true: one future assertion that tolerates a valid ledger - asserting
     `errors.some(...)` where another error already exists, say - would be silent, and the

The digest pair 4c219f5f guarded keeps its explicit assertion AND routes through mutate().
Criterion 3 honoured: no fixture under src/testing/fixtures/ledgers/ was swept to the live pin.
c42f9ac2... still appears there after am-cf6m because those are fixture values, not the pin -
which is also the judgement I made when I left them alone in 9d3122ef.

CRITERION 4, the same scan elsewhere. RULE: a test file that reads from disk (readFileSync,
loadFixture, readFile) AND calls .replace/.replaceAll with a literal first argument.

    files: 17      such calls: 28

      5  src/content/kernel/verifyContentKernelBinding.test.ts
      4  src/testing/bm06Session.test.mjs
      3  src/testing/editions/miniPaperContract.test.ts     [already guarded]
      2  src/equations/missingStep/contentCheck.test.mjs
      2  src/testing/scenarios.coverage.test.ts
      1  each: scripts/e2e-edition-pipeline, scripts/e2e/uiExtraction.e2e,

            src/content/editions/brownian.inventory, src/reader/detail/emitReadings.integration,

ONE OF THOSE ROWS IS MY OWN SCANNER OVER-REPORTING. scripts/verify-facsimile-pins.test.ts is
listed unguarded, but the replacement I added there this session IS guarded - by

Whoever takes the other sixteen files should measure each the way I measured this one - neuter

title: The OCR guard's coverage test proves the denylist MENTIONS an engine, not that the guard refuses it
description:
Found by the am-o44v substring sweep, judging the 415 gating string-receiver sites in the
test population. This one guards the project's hardest resource rule - AGENTS.md, "NEVER RUN
OCR ON THIS MACHINE ... This prohibition is permanent and has no convenience, deadline,
fallback, or 'small batch' exception."

scripts/ocr-guard.test.ts:132-144, the test named
  "the three engines AGENTS.md names by name are all covered"

    const namedInPolicy = ["focr", "tesseract", "ocrmypdf"];
    const { denylist } = await loadDenylist(ROOT);
    const patterns = denylist.map((entry) => entry.pattern.toLowerCase());

    const uncovered = namedInPolicy.filter((tool) => !patterns.some((p) => p.includes(tool)));
    assert.deepEqual(uncovered, [], "AGENTS.md names these OCR engines and the denylist must too");

"Covered" is decided by whether some pattern STRING contains the tool's letters. The property
the test's own name claims is whether the GUARD REFUSES that engine, and the file already
imports the function that answers it.

The two are not the same, because a pattern's category decides which matchers get compiled.
scripts/sources/ocrGuard.ts compileMatchers only builds spawnRegex/binaryRegex for
category "binary-or-spawn" or "import-or-spawn"; a "dependency-or-import" entry compiles an
importRegex only. And scripts/ocr-guard-denylist.json holds BOTH shapes for the same engine:

    {"pattern": "tesseract.js",        "category": "dependency-or-import"}
    {"pattern": "node-tesseract-ocr",  "category": "dependency-or-import"}
    {"pattern": "tesseract",           "category": "binary-or-spawn"}

"tesseract.js".includes("tesseract") is true, so the coverage test is satisfied by the
dependency entry alone.

EXECUTED, node --experimental-strip-types, calling the real loadDenylist and
scanContentForViolations against the line `execSync("<tool> in.png out.txt");`:

  --- as shipped ---
    coverage test uncovered: []
    guard refuses execSync("focr ...")      : true
    guard refuses execSync("tesseract ...") : true
    guard refuses execSync("ocrmypdf ...")  : true

  --- with ONLY the binary-or-spawn "tesseract" entry removed ---
    coverage test uncovered: []      <- STILL PASSES
    guard refuses execSync("focr ...")      : true
    guard refuses execSync("tesseract ...") : FALSE
    guard refuses execSync("ocrmypdf ...")  : true

So the one test that ties the denylist back to the words of the policy goes green while the
guard stops refusing a local tesseract spawn. Nothing is escaping today - as shipped, all
three are genuinely refused. This is the gate being unable to notice the regression, not a
live escape.

SUGGESTED FIX, not applied: assert the category, not the letters. For each engine AGENTS.md
names, plant a spawn line and an import line and require scanContentForViolations to return a
violation. That is the function the test file already imports, it needs no new machinery, and
it fails for the right reason when a binary-or-spawn entry is dropped or recategorised. Keep
the existing assertion too if you want the denylist to stay legible; it is not wrong, it is
just not the claim in the test's name.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The coverage test drives scanContentForViolations, not a pattern-string substring.
- Planted negative: removing the binary-or-spawn "tesseract" entry turns the test RED.
- Other half: the denylist as shipped stays GREEN, and the three named engines are each
  refused for a spawn AND for an import.
- Both proofs driven red first, files restored byte-identical (cmp).

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text:
ORCHESTRATOR FOLLOW-THROUGH (TanElk). pane30 found that the coverage test proves the denylist MENTIONS an engine rather than that the guard REFUSES it. I asked the question the test declines to ask, by calling scanContentForViolations directly, and the answer is that the guard has a live hole in the most common invocation forms.

CALL FORMS, each scanned as src/content/foo.ts against the real loaded denylist:

    caught   spawn("tesseract", ["a.pdf"]);
    MISSED   spawnSync("tesseract", ["a.pdf"]);
    caught   execFile("tesseract", ["a.pdf"]);
    MISSED   execFileSync("tesseract", ["a.pdf"]);
    caught   execSync("tesseract a.pdf");
    MISSED   Bun.spawnSync(["tesseract", "a.pdf"]);

    correctly ignored: const engine = "tesseract";   (a bare mention is not a call)

ROOT CAUSE, exact. ocrGuard.ts:65-68:

    spawnRegex = new RegExp(
      `(?:spawn|exec|execSync|execFile|fork)\\s*\\(\\s*['\"\`]${escapeRegex(p)}['\"\`]`, "i")

The alternation carries execSync but NOT spawnSync, and not execFileSync. `spawn` does match
the first five letters of `spawnSync`, and then \s*\( fails against `Sync(`, so the whole
match fails. It is an omission in a hand-written alternation, not a design decision.
binaryRegex at :69-72 shares the same alternation and the same gap.

WHY THIS IS WORSE HERE THAN IT WOULD BE ELSEWHERE. This is a Bun repository.
`Bun.spawnSync(["tool", ...])` is the idiomatic way to launch a binary in it - the array
form with no separate command string - and it is invisible to every matcher. The repo's own
code uses argv-style spawning throughout (scripts/verify-facsimile-pins.ts calls
spawnSync("pdftoppm", [...])). So the form an author here would most naturally reach for to
run an OCR engine is precisely the form the guard cannot see.

THE TWO HALVES, in pane31's frame. The PREDICATE half is fine for the forms it covers and
the bare-mention control behaves correctly. The MEASURING half is incomplete, and the
coverage test cannot detect that because it never calls the matcher - it inspects the
denylist's strings. A test that asked 'does the guard refuse this engine, invoked the way
this repo invokes binaries' would have failed from the day spawnSync was omitted.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA I AM ADDING:
  5. The coverage test asserts REFUSAL by calling scanContentForViolations, for each engine
     AGENTS.md names, in every call form the repository actually uses - including
     spawnSync, execFileSync and Bun.spawnSync's array form.
  6. Planted negative per form: each form, with a denied engine, is refused; confirm each
     goes RED against the current code before the fix (three of them already do - they are
     the MISSED rows above, which is a fixture set that is known-reachable).
  7. Control: the bare-mention case stays UNREFUSED, so the fix does not turn the guard
     into a substring matcher over prose. That is the failure direction to avoid, and it is
     the one this whole sweep exists to prevent.

No OCR was run to produce any of this. Nothing was executed; strings were scanned.

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text:
pane28: DONE in d6bceb43 - scripts/sources/ocrGuard.ts and scripts/ocr-guard.test.ts. The denylist JSON is untouched. Reporting, not closing. AND THERE IS AN OWNER QUESTION AT THE BOTTOM THAT I DID NOT DECIDE.

CRITERION 6, REACHABILITY BEFORE REDNESS, exactly as you framed it. I wrote the refusal test first and ran it against the unfixed guard: RED, listing nine unrefused combinations - all THREE named engines times the three missed forms, not just tesseract. focr and ocrmypdf were equally invisible via spawnSync, execFileSync and Bun.spawnSync. So the known-reachable fixture set is larger than the three rows in your table; the rows were per form, and every form multiplies across every engine.

CRITERION 5. The coverage test now calls scanContentForViolations for each engine AGENTS.md names, in seven call forms taken from what this repository actually does: spawn, spawnSync, execFile, execFileSync, execSync, Bun.spawn array form, Bun.spawnSync array form. A separate test covers the import forms. I kept the old mentions-test, as the bead suggested - it is not wrong, it just is not the claim in its name.

CRITERION 7, AND THIS IS THE PART I TREATED AS THE CONSTRAINT RATHER THAN A CHECKBOX. The matcher still requires a launcher identifier, an opening parenthesis, and the denied name as a QUOTED ARGUMENT. The only widening is the alternation itself plus an optional `[` so the array form reaches the quote. `const engine = "tesseract"` stays unrefused, and so do a comment naming all three engines, a string that says focr is forbidden, and a template literal mentioning ocrmypdf - all four are in the control. PLANT C proves the control is load-bearing rather than decorative: degrading spawnRegex to a bare pattern turns it RED on `const engine = "tesseract";`. You were right that this is the failure direction that matters, and it is the one that would actually get the guard switched off.

ROOT CAUSE, confirming yours exactly. The alternation carried execSync and no other Sync variant; `spawn` matches the first five letters of `spawnSync` and the following \s*\( then fails against `Sync(`. Fixed by one named constant, PROCESS_LAUNCHERS, used by both spawnRegex and binaryRegex so they cannot drift apart again.

PLANT A, which is the bead's own claim demonstrated rather than argued: with the binary-or-spawn "tesseract" entry removed, my refusal test goes RED naming every tesseract call form - AND THE OLD MENTIONS-TEST STAYS GREEN, because "tesseract.js".includes("tesseract"). The two tests now sit in one file where the next reader can see the difference. PLANT B: padding the pin below with a violation that does not occur goes RED. All three plants restored byte-identically, verified with cmp.

THE OWNER QUESTION, WHICH IS WHY I AM FLAGGING RATHER THAN CLAIMING THIS IS FINISHED. With spawnSync visible, the repository scan finds exactly ONE violation in 2673 files: scripts/verify-facsimile-pins.ts:517, spawnSync("pdftotext", ...). Fixing the matcher did not create it - the guard has never once been able to see it, which is a second, quieter consequence of the same hole.

Both sides fairly:
  - the call reads folio numerals out of a parent scan's EXISTING text layer to check which printed page a parent page is. Its own header argues reading an existing layer is parsing, not recognition; AGENTS.md permits inspecting a pinned PDF; its output is integers for page identity and never becomes ledger or edition text.
  - the denylist entry is broader than its own stated reason. The pattern denies every call; the reason denies a USE - "pdftotext text-layer extraction is forbidden IN SOURCE-LAYER PIPELINES ... must not substitute for cloud OCR research drafts or editorial transcription."

What I did instead: the repository-scan test pins that one violation by file and pattern, says in the code that it is an open question and NOT an approval and NOT an exemption mechanism, still fails on any other violation anywhere in the tree, and FAILS IF THE PIN GOES STALE, so a resolved question cannot quietly become standing permission. If you would rather the scan simply go red until the owner rules, say so and I will make it red - that is a one-line change and I will not argue with it.

A THIRD FINDING, dead-escape class. DenylistConfig declares allowedRenderers with a pattern and a reason, ocr-guard-denylist.json populates it with pdftoppm and pdfjs-dist, and NOTHING READS IT - one occurrence in ocrGuard.ts, the type declaration. pdftoppm is permitted only because it is absent from the denylist, not because the allowance is honoured. Same shape as am-uj6w: a documented escape that no code consumes. Not fixed, not in scope, and it matters here because the obvious way to "resolve" the pdftotext question is to add it to a list that does nothing.

title: Every build fetches a font over the network for the Open Graph star glyph and gets HTTP 400
description:
Every production build prints, during Open Graph image generation:

    Failed to load dynamic font for ✦ . Error: [Error: Failed to download dynamic font. Status: 400]

Observed in two consecutive builds tonight (2026-09-20, both exit 0), so it is not a
transient. The glyph is U+2726 BLACK FOUR POINTED STAR, at src/app/opengraph-image.tsx:72,
inside the red 48x48 mark at the top left of the share card.

## Why this is more than a noisy line

src/app/opengraph-image.tsx passes no `fonts` option to ImageResponse - the options
object is `{ ...size }` - so next/og falls back to FETCHING A FONT OVER THE NETWORK for
any glyph its built-in font does not cover. That fetch is what returns 400.

Two consequences, and the first is the one that matters:

1. THE BUILD REACHES THE NETWORK FOR A FONT. The file's own header says, as a recorded
   modification from the donor, "Removed all third-party external fonts and CDN
   requests; uses system serif/monospace fonts and inline styling" and "Adheres strictly
   to ... local-only asset policy." That claim is false at build time for this glyph. It
   is a build-time request rather than a reader-facing one, so
   src/testing/thirdPartyRequests.test.ts and the browser network check in
   scripts/e2e/uiExtraction.e2e.test.ts both pass and neither can see it - they scan the
   sources and watch the reader's browser, not the builder's.

2. THE GLYPH MAY NOT BE RENDERING. The fetch fails, so whatever next/og substitutes is
   what ships in the card. The PNG is still valid - verified, 8950 4e47, and the browser
   acceptance passes the Open Graph check - but nobody has looked at what is inside the
   red square.

## Not yet established

Whether the emitted card shows the star, a tofu box, or nothing. That is a five-minute
look at out/opengraph-image and it should be the first step, because it decides whether
this is a cosmetic defect plus a policy violation, or only the latter.

## Provenance

Found by pane28 in the build log while rebuilding out/ for the am-ahyb browser
acceptance. Not caused by that work; it predates it and recurs on every build.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The build emits no "Failed to download dynamic font" line, and the fix is either a
  glyph the built-in font covers or a locally bundled font passed through the `fonts`
  option - not a suppressed warning.
- Evidence that the emitted card renders the intended mark: the region is inspected in
  the generated PNG before and after, and both are recorded.
- The file's header claim about no third-party font requests is true afterwards, or the
  claim is corrected to match what the code does.
- Planted negative that goes RED: a glyph outside the available coverage reintroduces
  the warning and is caught by a gate, rather than only by a human reading build output.
  Confirm that state is reachable first - it is reachable today, which is this bead.
- Control: out/opengraph-image remains a valid PNG of the declared size and the Open
  Graph browser check in scripts/e2e/uiExtraction.e2e.test.ts still passes in both engines.
close_reason: Completed. 1 (build emits no dynamic-font line): the production build log of live 254d3459 (scratchpad/deploy/build-254d3459.log, 460 lines, stdout and stderr) has 0 'dynamic font' and 0 'Failed to load' lines. The verified deploy's own vercel build log (656 lines) also has 0 and 0. The same grep over all 29 build logs from 2026-09-23 on finds 0, so every one postdates the fix. The positive control for the wording is NavyKite's: putting the ✦ back in shareCards turns the font check red and brings back 'Failed to load dynamic font'. The fix is local fonts: renderShareCard passes fonts: cardFonts(), the self-hosted faces, for every card. 2 (the mark): NavyKite inspected all six live PNGs, with no star and no missing-glyph box. Audit on the bead at 2026-09-24T15:00:59Z.

title: Ten outline and navigation link names still map to more than one destination
description:
Residual class left after am-xbfm fixed the passage action bar. Measured by rendering the real PaperReader to static markup at fc29bf3 and comparing each link accessible name against the set of destinations it points to:

```
distinct link names on the Brownian reader : 112
names mapping to MORE THAN ONE destination :  10

  "In words"                         -> 5 destinations
  "Explanation"                      -> 2
  "Section-only reading ->"          -> 2
  "Zero average is not no movement"  -> 2
  "Why the square grows with time"   -> 2
  "From a step law to a density law" -> 2
  "What the spreading curve predicts"-> 2
  "Why viscosity changes the spread" -> 2
```

am-xbfm eliminated the large offenders in the passage action bar (6x "Try it", 6x "Why?", 6x "Show the missing step", 40x "Read the prerequisite"). These ten are outline and navigation links, which fall outside that bead scope line, so they are recorded here rather than by widening it after the fact.

## Triage before fixing - several may be fine

A section outline entry and an inline heading link that both point at the same section under the same title are not a defect. Only a name that resolves to genuinely different destinations misleads. "In words" at 5 destinations is the one that looks clearly wrong.

## Acceptance

1. For each of the ten, a recorded determination: are the destinations genuinely different pages/anchors, or the same target reached two ways? Cite the hrefs.
2. Every name whose destinations genuinely differ is made distinguishable, carrying the section or passage it belongs to. Visible text may stay short; use aria-label as PassageActionsBar already does.
3. Re-measure with the same method and record the table; names whose destinations differ must all be at one destination each.
4. A negative a naive fix would fail: two different sections offering the same action type must not end up with the same accessible name.

## No-claim

Unique names do not prove the names are good, nor that reading order is sensible. No manual screen-reader review has been performed.

## Provenance

Measured by orchestrator TanElk on 2026-09-17 while verifying am-xbfm, by rendering the component rather than reading the diff.

title: glossConventions classifies an error by its message text, produced in another module, so a reword silently downgrades a validation failure
description:
src/content/schemas/glossConventions.ts:64 decides whether a caught error is a
VALIDATION failure to rethrow or an IO failure to downgrade, by matching the
error's message text:

    if (message.includes("is not a valid GlossNoteClass")) {
      throw err;
    }
    warnings.push(`Error reading ${resolvedPath}: ${message}`);
    return { modalityClasses: DEFAULT_MODALITY_CLASSES, ... };

The message it matches is produced in a DIFFERENT MODULE,
src/content/schemas/glossConventions.pure.ts:64, as an interpolated template
with no shared constant between them.

## The failure

Reword that message - a typo fix, a clearer phrasing, a translation - and this
branch stops firing. The validation error is then swallowed into a warning and
the loader silently returns DEFAULT_MODALITY_CLASSES. An invalid gloss-class
configuration would degrade to defaults instead of failing, and the only trace
is a warning line.

Fail-open, cross-module, and coupled through prose that nothing marks as
load-bearing. Nobody editing the message in the pure module has any signal that
a catch block three files away depends on its wording.

## The fix, which this repository already uses elsewhere

Throw a typed error and check the type, not the prose. src/experiments/bm07/
kitchen/protocol.ts carries the pattern: `throw new TypeError(msg, { cause: {
code: "kebab-code" } })`, and the consumer branches on the code. Either that or
an exported error class.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. The classification is by type or by a stable code, not by message text.
2. BOTH HALVES: an invalid GlossNoteClass still propagates rather than
   degrading to defaults, AND a genuine IO failure - a missing or unreadable
   conventions file - still downgrades to a warning with the defaults, which is
   the behaviour the catch exists for.
3. A planted negative that would have caught this: change the message text in
   glossConventions.pure.ts and the rethrow must still happen.

## Provenance

Found by pane30 (BrightIsland) in band C of am-o44v, the residue with no
category word within five lines. Second site in that band to falsify the
filter's proxy: no category vocabulary anywhere near it, and it is deciding a
category.

src/experiments/lifecycle/recovery.ts:261-265
    if (message.includes("length")) mismatchField = "trailing-bytes";
    else if (message.includes("magic")) mismatchField = "magic";
    else if (message.includes("domain")) mismatchField = "domain";
  Classifies a checkpoint decode failure by the decoder's message text.
  Lower consequence than the gloss one: the ACTION is new-run either way, so a
  misclassification produces a wrong diagnostic label rather than wrong
  behaviour. But mismatchField is exactly the sort of value that ends up in the
  structured logs AGENTS.md requires, and a wrong field there is a measurement

src/content/schemas/strictParse.ts:153
    const code = e.message.toLowerCase().includes("duplicate key") ? ... 
  Derives a refusal CODE from message prose, which is the inversion of the
  pattern the rest of the repository uses - bm07/kitchen/protocol.ts throws
  with { cause: { code } } and the consumer branches on the code.

All three sites share one root: an error's category is carried in its prose
rather than its type, so the producer and the consumer are coupled through
text that nothing marks as load-bearing.

title: 105 refusal codes converted in batches 1-4 carry no targeted test
description:
Owed by me, from batches 1-4 of the am-p465 kebab migration, under the owner's ruling that the
migration tests what it converts. These predate that ruling; batch 5 onward converts and tests
in the same batch. This does not block batch 5.

THE BEAD TITLE SAYS 105 AND HERE IS THE RULE THAT PRODUCED IT, because titles in this repo have
been off by 15-20x and fe131243's "130" was a different denominator - it was the untested-refusal
ratchet's file-level count at that moment, not a site count.

    RULE converted: a site that throws or fails with a KEBAB LITERAL -
                    `throw new XxxError("kebab", ...)` or `fail("kebab", ...)`
    RULE tested:    that code is ASSERTED ON in a *.test.* file - toBe / toEqual /
                    assert.equal / .code, "..." / refusalCode, "..." / toContain

    converted sites                                     152
      code asserted on in a test                         47
      OWED                                              105

    A looser rule - the code string merely APPEARS anywhere in a test file - gives 56 tested
    and 96 owed. I am reporting the strict number as the headline because a mention is not a
    test, and reporting both because the gap between them (9 codes) is the size of the
    over-count a looser rule would have produced.

PER FILE, owed of converted:

     1 of  15  scripts/sources/supersedePin.ts
    11 of  32  scripts/download-facsimiles.ts
     4 of   8  scripts/verify-facsimile-pins.ts
     1 of   1  src/experiments/shelf/definition.ts
     3 of   5  src/experiments/shelf/session.ts
     2 of   2  src/experiments/shelf/settings.ts
     2 of   3  src/experiments/avogadro/session.ts
     3 of   4  src/experiments/lightThread/session.ts
     1 of   1  src/experiments/lq06/changes.ts
     3 of   5  src/experiments/lq06/session.ts
    32 of  32  src/experiments/bm07/kitchen/csv.ts
    14 of  14  src/experiments/bm07/kitchen/schema.ts
    11 of  11  src/equations/derivations/exactSeries.ts
    10 of  10  src/equations/derivations/massEnergyLowSpeed.ts
     1 of   1  src/equations/derivations/lowSpeedState.ts
     1 of   1  src/equations/derivations/renderLowSpeed.ts
     2 of   2  src/components/lab/avogadro/AvogadroLab.tsx
     2 of   2  src/components/lab/lightThread/LightThreadLab.tsx
     1 of   1  src/discovery/lightQuanta/controls.ts

WHERE THE DEBT CONCENTRATES: 67 of the 105 are in four files - the kitchen pair (46) and the two
derivation helpers (21). Those four are also the ones where a test is cheapest, because each
refusal is reachable by feeding one bad value to one exported function. The scattered singletons
in the lab components are the expensive ones, because reaching them needs a rendered component
with a refused snapshot.

TWO LIMITS OF THESE NUMBERS, stated rather than found later:
  1. The converted count misses RETURNED codes. scripts/sources/facsimileSourceSchema.ts shows
     zero sites because its refusals are returned as { refusalCode }, not thrown, and the SITE
     rule reads throw/fail only. Batch 1 converted 74 quoted literals in that file. So 152 is a
     floor for "converted", not a total.
  2. "Asserted on" is a text rule over test sources. A test that asserts the code via a variable,
     or checks a refusal without naming its code, reads as owed here and may not be.

Both limits push in the same direction as every text instrument I have built tonight: the owed
number is an upper bound and the tested number a lower one.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Each of the 105 sites is either covered by a test that asserts its code, or removed.
- The count is re-derived by the same two rules and stated in the closing comment, with the
  loose and strict numbers both given.
- No baseline entry is added, raised, or used as a substitute for a test.

title: The citation audit's site model does not match how this repo writes refusals: 362 allowed across 41 files, and widening the regex alone makes accurate citations read as false findings
description:
MEASURED, not estimated.

staleCitationsBaseline.json: 41 files, 362 allowed non-checking-out citations. experiment.ts alone allows 134, source.ts 57, reconciliation.ts 50. So 'citation debt is zero' means zero REGRESSIONS against a baseline of 362, not zero stale citations. Same qualification shape as '1973 of 2050 citations are visible to the audit'.

THE ROOT CAUSE, found by pane28 via dry run rather than argument.

The audit's notion of a 'site' is scanRefusalThrowSites, which counts ONLY:
    throw new SomeError('kebab-code')
The repository's citations mean 'the line that refuses', which in practice is three forms:
  1. coded throws        throw new XError('kebab-code')   - modelled
  2. bare throws         throw new Error('...')           - NOT modelled
  3. return-style        return { ok: false, code: 'x' }  - NOT modelled

parse.ts has 21 bare throws and 2 coded. aliases.ts and paperRoutes.ts are return-style. Their citations resolve to a real refusal line and the audit then finds no site there, so an ACCURATE citation is recorded as one that does not check out.

WHY THE OBVIOUS FIX IS WRONG, with evidence.

Widening the citation REGEX without widening the site MODEL converts invisible-but-accurate citations into visible-but-FALSE findings in at least twelve files. Each would then need its baseline RAISED for a citation that is already correct. Raising a baseline to accommodate a false positive is the shape of a weakened gate, so this path is refused.

pane28 also dry-ran the principled variant - accept any 'throw new *Error(' line, not just coded ones - and it is worse: 3 failures including the scan-root test and the tightening-pawl test, so it perturbs the untested-refusal side as well. Restored byte-identically after.

WHAT THIS ITEM ACTUALLY IS.

Not a regex change. A change to what counts as a refusal site, which changes what am-ksl3 promises and what the 362 baseline means. Doing it properly means:
  - decide whether bare throws and return-style refusals are sites
  - if yes, re-derive every one of the 41 baselines from the new model
  - plant against all three refusal forms, both directions
  - state the new denominator the way the old one was stated

DO NOT start this by editing the regex. The two blind-spot mechanisms are real and were verified independently at refusalScanner.ts:751, :778, :779, but they are HARMLESS: no citation has been found that is both invisible and stale. A documented blind spot is better than a manufactured false positive.

Owner decision required before any code.
notes:
CORRECTION TO THIS BEAD'S CENTRAL PREMISE. Found by pane28 in b20d07af; recorded by TanElk, who wrote the wrong version here.

THIS BEAD SAYS the audit's site model is 'throw new SomeError(kebab-code)' ONLY, and that return-style refusals are unmodelled. THAT IS FALSE.

scanRefusalThrowSites has TWO patterns and always has:

    Pattern 1   throw new <Error>("kebab-code")
    Pattern 2   a standalone code:/kind:/rule:/refusalCode:/errorCode: field carrying
                a kebab string - which is how a RETURNED refusal record counts

MEASURED repo-wide: 2115 sites, 1406 reached from a throw and 709 from a returned record. A THIRD of the population is the shape this bead said was out of scope.

HOW BOTH OF US GOT IT WRONG. pane28 took the model from the ratchet's own SCOPE NOTE rather than from the scanner, reported it to me, and I wrote it onto this bead and onto am-r3qt as established fact. It was then used to classify 362 citation findings. The note was wrong and neither of us read the implementation it described. That is the proxy failure this whole session has been about - a comment standing in for the code - committed by the two people policing it.

pane28 found it by opening editionContract.ts to plant its five untested sites and discovering that four of the five are  - returned records, not throws. Twelve of that file's thirteen sites are Pattern 2.

WHAT SURVIVES, and it is worth separating carefully because two different functions are involved:

  - The CITATION-MATCHING mechanisms I verified independently at refusalScanner.ts:751, :778 and :779 - the parenthesised-form requirement, and the test/it split eating a citation's opening bracket - are UNAFFECTED. Those are about how a citation is read, not about what counts as a site. They still stand.
  - The SITE-MODEL claim - 'coded throws only' - is withdrawn. Return-style refusals ARE modelled, by Pattern 2.
  - The LINE-EXACTNESS requirement recorded here (a site must be a RANGE, not a line, because ]); and } are the middle of multi-line constructs) is UNAFFECTED and still the binding constraint on any fix.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE 362 BREAKDOWN recorded on this bead (~101 one-line convention difference, ~46 code-mismatched, ~53 genuine rot): it was computed against a site model believed to be throws-only. It must be RE-DERIVED against the real two-pattern model before anyone acts on it. Do not treat those three numbers as measured until that is done.

am-r3qt carries the same false premise and needs the same correction.

comments.text:

I classified 48 to 63 of the 362 citation findings as 'return-style refusals the

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text:
A THIRD EMISSION SHAPE THE SITE MODEL MISSES, found by planting rather than by reading.

src/content/editions/editionContract.ts emits digest-mismatch four ways:

    776    code: ok ? undefined : "digest-mismatch"        Pattern 2, COUNTED
    934    check1Code = "digest-mismatch";                  NOT COUNTED
    945    check1Code = "digest-mismatch";                  NOT COUNTED
    1016   code: failed ? "digest-mismatch" : undefined     Pattern 2, COUNTED

Pattern 2 matches a code:/kind:/rule:/refusalCode:/errorCode: FIELD. An
assignment to a variable that is later used as the code is not a field, so
934 and 945 are invisible.

PLANTED BOTH WAYS, same file, same test run:

    plant 776 and 1016 (the counted sites)   0 tests redden
    plant 934 and 945 (the uncounted ones)   2 tests redden, both asserting
                                             c.code === "digest-mismatch"

So for this code the census points at the two sites NOBODY drives and misses
the two that ARE driven. It undercounts the population and misattributes within
it, in the same file, simultaneously.

(counted), variable assignment (NOT counted), accumulator (NOT counted). My
earlier retraction said only the accumulator was outside; that was still too
generous to the model.

site would not have caught 934 either, because the problem there is not the

title: Refusal coverage instruments are structurally blind to 1064 of 2617 throw sites (bare throws carry no code string)
description:
Established by pane28 on am-muyh after three requests for an honest denominator. This is the fourth bead premise this session found materially wrong, and the most consequential.

THE DENOMINATOR, as reported:
  total throw sites                2617
  planted and confirmed            1284   a plant was applied and a reaching test went red
  covered by test without a plant   250   a reaching test names the code; never planted, so never confirmed
  unreachable, with reason            1   parse.ts:542, getInfixPrecedence returns the floor for every token the branches above it do not handle, so no input reaches it
  never planted, no claim at all   1082   ~1064 bare throws with no code string, 5 coded sites no test names, 13 in modules no test imports

Confirmed covered is 1052, not 1302. 49 percent of sites have been planted.

THE DEFECT IS THE INSTRUMENT, NOT THE COVERAGE. About 1064 throw sites are bare throws carrying no code string. Every name-based instrument in this repo - including the refusal ratchet's own scanner - matches on code strings, so it is STRUCTURALLY SILENT on 41 percent of the population it purports to measure. Those sites are not reported as uncovered; they are not reported at all. A ratchet that cannot see two fifths of its domain is not a ratchet over that domain.

For context on how far the original framing was off: am-muyh's title says '121 of 391 refusal codes are named by no test'. The real universe is 2617 sites. The 391 figure counts CODES, and a code is not a throw site - pane28 established early that the unit must be the throw site and the only instrument is the planted negative, because name matching had scored six sites as covered that no test exercised.

WHAT IS NEEDED: an instrument that does not depend on a code string. Candidates worth evaluating rather than assuming - AST-level enumeration of throw statements with their enclosing function and module, so identity comes from location rather than payload; coverage instrumentation that records which throw statements were reached during a run; or a lint that forbids new bare throws in the refusal path so the population stops growing while the existing block is worked down. Whichever is chosen must report the bare-throw block as MEASURED rather than absent.

ACCEPTANCE: a report that accounts for all 2617 sites with no silent class, and a ratchet whose scanner covers the bare-throw population or declares explicitly that it does not and how many it is excluding. Do not close am-muyh against the old 391-code framing - that number measures the wrong thing.

CREDIT: pane28 produced this only after I asked three times, and it is the right answer to the question rather than a number that would have closed the bead. Its earlier finding on the same bead - that name matching had scored six throw sites as covered when no test exercised them - is the same defect at smaller scale.

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text:
pane28: TWO MORE ABSENT POPULATIONS, confirmed on pane29's lead, plus the refusal-path question this bead will need answered.

SCOPE. findSourceFiles takes ONE directory and every caller passes 'src' (refusalScanner.ts lines 216 and 451). It also skips anything under a testing/ directory. So neither refusal instrument has ever seen:

  scripts/**       388 bare,  36 coded refusal sites, 130 files
  src/testing/**    84 bare,  28 coded refusal sites,  69 files

472 bare and 64 coded sites, ABSENT rather than zero. Confirmed by walking both trees with the same two detectors the instruments use.

I fixed my own half in b0a7d08. scanBareThrows now walks src and scripts with its own walk, does not skip testing/, reports per-root totals every run, enters a root in the report even when it contributes nothing, and asserts every declared root was walked with a positive file count. Narrowing the roots back to src alone now FAILS the gate as slack. Census: 1490 bare in 362 files, 1896 coded, across 1328 files.

I did NOT widen the coded scanner (analyzeUntestedRefusals). Adding those 64 coded sites would put unknown-coverage sites under refusalRatchet's baseline of zeros and likely fail it on work nobody has been asked to do. That is this bead's call, not a side effect of mine. The numbers above are what it would cost.

THE OTHER HALF OF THE INSTRUMENT PROBLEM, which this bead should own too: of the bare throws, how many are in the refusal path at all? Doctrine 8 binds a throw where a reader should have received a typed refusal; it does not bind a parser's internal invariant. The scanner CANNOT SEPARATE THEM. It matches 'throw new X(' and subtracts coded lines; it has no caller analysis and no notion of reader-supplied input. Reported as an instrument finding, not worked around.

How far it can be pushed without that analysis:
  - Full population, by thrown class: 279 of 1018 (27.4%) throw a PROJECT-DEFINED Error subclass
    across 54 classes (TapeValidationError 67, KitchenInputError 41, ExportValidationError 24,
    ParseError 21, ...). Nobody defines KitchenInputError for an internal invariant, so 279 is a
    measured LOWER BOUND on the refusal path. 739 throw a built-in Error/TypeError/RangeError and
    are genuinely ambiguous. (Figures predate the scope widening; the ratio, not the total.)
  - A sample of 30 I read with context, systematic every-34th and NOT random: roughly 14 refusal
    path (pasted CSV, authored YAML, a permalink tape, an offline manifest, reader-typed numerics
    rejecting NaN), roughly 8 internal invariants (React context misuse, 'Expected pooled buffer',
    'Missing comparison cell', a dev-only storage guard), roughly 8 unclassifiable from the call
    site. At n=30 that is about plus or minus 18 points and I will not scale it to the population.

THREE WAYS TO SETTLE IT, in increasing cost: split the census by thrown class (free, twenty lines, turns one opaque block into 279/739); mark the refusal path in source with a tag or a shared base class the scanner reads (the only approach yielding a number nobody defends with a sample, and it changes how every refusal is written, so it is an owner decision); or caller analysis from the entry points, which is the RSC gate's machinery and still cannot see which inputs are reader-supplied.

comments.author: TanElk
comments.text:
OWNER DECISION SURFACED by pane28, plus one option I am authorising without you.

THE INSTRUMENT'S OWN LIMIT, reported rather than worked around: the scanner matches 'throw new X(' and subtracts coded lines. It has no caller analysis and no notion of reader-supplied input. Doctrine 8 binds only the reader-facing case, so the census counts a MIXTURE of reader-facing refusals and internal invariants, and the gate can honestly claim only 'unmeasured by the code-based scanner'.

WHAT IS MEASURED: 279 of 1018 bare throws (27.4%) throw a project-defined Error subclass across 54 classes - TapeValidationError 67, KitchenInputError 41, ExportValidationError 24, ParseError 21. Nobody defines KitchenInputError for an internal invariant, so 279 is a measured LOWER BOUND on the refusal-path population. The remaining 739 are built-in Error, TypeError and RangeError, and are genuinely ambiguous from the throw site alone.

WHAT IS SAMPLED, with its uncertainty stated: a systematic every-34th sample of 30 read with call-site context gave roughly 14 refusal path, 8 internal invariants, 8 unclassifiable. Pane28's own words: 'At n=30 that's plus or minus 18 points; I won't scale it.' It computed the interval and declined to extrapolate. That is the correct handling and I am recording it so nobody later treats the sample as a population figure.

THREE WAYS TO SETTLE IT:
1. Split the census by thrown class. Free, about 20 lines, turns one opaque block of 1018 into 279 measured plus 739 ambiguous. I AM AUTHORISING THIS NOW - it strictly increases what is measured, changes no source, and needs nobody's permission.
2. Mark the refusal path in source with a tag or a shared base class the scanner reads. This is the ONLY approach that yields a number nobody has to defend with a sample. It is the OWNER'S CALL because it changes how every refusal in the codebase is written.
3. Caller analysis from the entry points. This is the RSC gate's machinery and it still cannot see which inputs are reader-supplied, so it does not settle the question.

MY READ: option 2 is the real answer and option 1 is worth doing regardless, because it shrinks the ambiguous block before anyone decides. Option 3 buys little for its cost.

Recording that this does NOT disturb the am-muyh closure: that bead closed for its CODED scope with zero untested coded sites, and the bare block was explicitly recorded as not done and tracked here. This refines this bead's scope, which is where it belongs.

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text:
pane28: OPTION 1 SHIPPED, commit 3919699. Option 2 left with the owner, option 3 not pursued.

I am again acting on a truncated instruction: the message reached me beginning mid-word at '...r's call'. What survived intact was that option 2 is the owner's, option 3 buys little, and the 279 must be labelled a measured lower bound wherever it appears and never a total. Option 1 was the only actionable item left, and it is the one I had offered to do on request, so that is what I built. Say so if the missing part asked for something else.

THE CENSUS NOW SPLITS THE BLOCK:
  366 of 1490 bare throws use a PROJECT-DEFINED error class, across 68 classes
      TapeValidationError 67, KitchenInputError 41, FacsimileError 34,
      ExportValidationError 24, ParseError 21, and 63 more
  1124 use a built-in class and are UNCLASSIFIED

NUMBER DISCIPLINE, since the figure moved. The 279 of 1018 I reported earlier was measured BEFORE scripts/ and src/testing/ entered the census. Post-widening the same ratio reads 366 of 1490. Both are MEASURED LOWER BOUNDS on the refusal path; neither is a total, and the two should not be quoted as a before/after improvement, because nothing improved - the population got measured.

WHY IT IS A LOWER BOUND AND NOT AN ESTIMATE. Nobody defines KitchenInputError for an internal invariant, so a project-defined class is good evidence of refusal path. The converse does not hold: the 1124 built-in throws certainly contain more refusals. Unclassified is not the same as not a refusal, and the census says exactly that in its own output every run.

THE LABEL IS ENFORCED, not just written. Three assertions hold the framing, and they make the bound two-sided:
  - lower bound + unclassified must sum to the bare total, so no site falls out of both classes;
  - the bound must be ABOVE zero, because zero means a broken classifier rather than a codebase
    with no refusal classes;
  - the bound must stay BELOW the total, so on the day it equals one the framing is revisited
    instead of quietly holding and turning a lower bound into a total by arithmetic;
  - the per-class breakdown must account for every project-class site.

Denominator check, four plants in an isolated copy, each caught: classifier forced to built-in, classifier forced to project, a site counted in neither class, a class dropped from the breakdown. Restored 4 pass 0 fail. I am not claiming which specific assertion fired for each plant - node prints a code frame that includes neighbouring assertion text, which made my tag detection unreliable. The verdicts are real; the attribution is not.

STILL THE OWNER'S CALL, unchanged: option 2, a tag or a shared base class every reader-facing refusal extends, is the only route to a number nobody has to defend with a sample. Until then the honest statement is 'at least 366 of 1490, and the rest is unmeasured', and the instruments should keep saying so.

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text:
pane28: CAN THE AMBIGUOUS BLOCK BE NARROWED WITHOUT SOURCE TAGGING? Partly. Measured, not argued.

FIRST, A NUMBER CORRECTION. The split is no longer 279 measured plus 739 ambiguous. Those were the src-only figures over a population of 1018, taken BEFORE b0a7d08 widened the census to scripts/ and src/testing/. Post-widening the artifact reports 366 project-defined and 1124 built-in, of 1490. Nothing improved between those two readings; the population got measured. Both project-class figures are lower bounds.

Also worth stating plainly: the census lands in TEST OUTPUT, not in a written artifact. bareThrowRatchet.test.ts console.logs it every run; nothing writes it to artifacts/. If a durable artifact is wanted that is a separate small piece of work.

TWO CHEAP SIGNALS, measured over all 1124 built-in bare throws:
  enclosing function takes an  parameter :  134
  enclosing function name is validate/parse/assert/admit/decode/check/load/... : 304
  EITHER signal present                           :  361  (32.1%)
  NEITHER                                         :  763  (67.9%)

PRECISION, spot-checked. The unknown-parameter group is the good one. Sampling 12 of the 134: parseLegacySpellingEntries, validateInline, checkCsvSize on a pasted observation CSV, decodeKitchenResponse, parseOfflineManifest, a notebook revision digest, parseNotebookDocument, parseCountermodelCase, validateAliases -- ten of twelve read as unambiguous refusal path. The two that do not are worker-host concurrency guards (receive: 'A recording owner cannot serve another instance'), where the caller is our own scheduler, so they are arguably invariants.

The unknown-parameter signal is the only PRINCIPLED one of the two: a parameter typed  means the type system explicitly cannot vouch for the value, which is the validation boundary itself. The name heuristic is lexical and weaker; it would carry 304 sites on the strength of spelling.

The NEITHER group reads invariant-heavy, which is the right direction for it: useGraphDescription outside its provider, a reading-only worker guard, relativeLuminance on a malformed hex, and the lab-page prepared-parameter guards, which check a build artifact rather than reader input.

THE HONEST ANSWER. Yes, about a third of the ambiguous block can be moved on cheap evidence, and the 134 unknown-parameter sites can be moved on good evidence. No, this cannot close the gap: 763 sites, 68% of the block, have neither signal and stay unresolved, and everything above is a THIRD PROXY stacked on the first two. It is a better-justified partition, not evidence about callers.

MY RECOMMENDATION, which is not a decision. Land the unknown-parameter count as a SECOND, tighter lower bound beside the 366, and do NOT land the name heuristic: 304 sites classified by spelling would dilute the one number in this census that is currently defensible. If that is wanted, say so; it is a small change to the census output plus its assertions. Source tagging remains the only route to a figure nobody defends with a proxy.

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text:
pane28: SECOND LOWER BOUND LANDED, commit fdf4042b. The census now reads:

  LOWER BOUND 500 of 1490, from two disjoint signals
    366  project-defined error class
    134  enclosing function takes an unknown-typed parameter
    990  reached by neither, still UNCLASSIFIED

TWO THINGS I GOT WRONG AND FIXED, both worth recording.

First, I broke a peer test. A peer had moved the relational assertions off the live tree and onto a fixture they build and control, with a comment explaining that live-tree existence claims hold only while the codebase happens to contain the right shapes, and fail naming the classifier when the truth is that the tree changed. That is a better design than mine. My first attempt added a live-tree existence assertion into that path, and it failed on their synthetic fixture, correctly. The second bound is now exercised from their fixture by construction instead.

Second, a planted negative passed and should not have. The double-count plant - tallying the unknown signal on project sites too - left the suite green, because no fixture site was BOTH project-class and unknown-param, so the disjointness assertion had nothing to bite on. comments.author: TanElk
comments.text:
A PLANTED NEGATIVE THAT PASSED WHEN IT SHOULD HAVE FAILED - pane28 found this in its own work and it is the subtlest failure mode this swarm has hit.

Pane28's words: 'The double-count plant - tallying the unknown signal on project sites too - left the suite green, because no fixture site was both project-class and unknown-param. The disjointness assertion was vacuous.'

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN AN ORDINARY BUG: a vacuous plant is indistinguishable from a working one by its result. Both are green. The whole point of a planted negative is that it goes red when the property breaks, and this one could not go red because no fixture exercised the overlap it was meant to detect. It was proof-shaped and proved nothing. Every other reward-hacking pattern in AGENTS.md leaves a trace - a weakened assertion, a regenerated golden, a tautological test you can read. A vacuous plant leaves a PASSING TEST that looks like evidence.

The fix was a fourth fixture file that makes the overlap possible, with a comment recording why it exists so nobody deletes it as redundant - which is exactly how it would be lost.

ALL FIVE PLANTS NOW CAUGHT: signal forced true, signal forced false, double-counted, residue arithmetic broken, signature lookback narrowed to zero.

THE GENERAL RULE THIS ESTABLISHES, and it applies to every plant in this repo including the ones I accepted this session: a plant is only evidence if the fixture can actually reach the state being planted. Verify the plant FAILS before you trust that it passes. I have accepted several planted negatives today on the strength of a red-then-green transition; that transition is the right check, and pane28 has now shown what it looks like when the red half is unreachable.

Success logs, not refusals. That precision fix is a separate gate diff and I did not bundle it.

- roots narrowed back to [src]: 5 pass 2 fail, caught twice over.
- includeTestingDirs dropped at the analyser's call site: PASSED my first scope pawl, because it asserted the WALK reaches testing/ and said nothing about whether the ANALYSIS asked it to. Only the slack pawl caught it. I added a file-count equality assertion; re-planted, 5 pass 2 fail. My own gate had the hole, and the plant is the only reason I know.

NOW THE QUESTION YOU ACTUALLY ASKED - does this make the coded refusal the path of least resistance? NO, and no scope change can. Three measurements, all at 8c2e4e73:

1. THE IDIOM IS NOT AT HAND WHERE THE BARE THROWS ARE. Of 1505 bare throw sites, 122 (8.1 percent) sit in a file that already uses a coded refusal, across 28 files. The other 1383 (91.9 percent) are in 336 files with NO coded refusal anywhere in them. An author writing a refusal in those 336 files has no local example to copy. Availability is the obstacle, not indifference.

2. THREE QUARTERS OF THEM ARE LANGUAGE BUILT-INS. Error 668, TypeError 321, RangeError 145 = 1134 of 1505. There is no project idiom in play at all for those.

3. THE PROJECT'S OWN TYPED ERROR CLASSES DO NOT PRODUCE CODED REFUSALS. The remaining 371 use 68 distinct bespoke classes - TapeValidationError 67, KitchenInputError 46, FacsimileError 34, ExportValidationError 24, and a long tail. KitchenInputError is the clean case: its constructor is (row: number, field: string, message: string), so an author who does everything right, defines a typed error class and throws it, still lands in the bare block, because there is no machine-readable code in the signature. That is not laziness; the class was written before any of this existed.

In scripts before this commit, coded cost NOTHING because this gate could not see it - so the widening removed a free ride rather than creating one. The ordering coded-cheaper-than-bare holds everywhere and is unchanged. What is missing is the thing no scope change supplies: one importable form that is SHORTER to write than 'throw new Error(...)' and that the scanner reads by construction. Re-ran two minutes later: 9 pass / 0 fail. Re-ran again: 9 pass / 0 fail, stable. Baseline sum now reads 16, and the census printed by the same run is src 9 untested + scripts 7 untested = 16 exactly. The file is committed and clean.

WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED: a pane was mid-way through landing a tightening from 18 to 16. Between the census dropping and the baseline commit arriving, the recorded baseline was genuinely slack against the real count, and the pawl correctly said so. It was right, briefly, about a state that lasted seconds.

THE SERIES IS ALL TIGHTENING: 24 to 22 to 18 to 16, every step a reduction, ratchet green at each settled point. Nobody loosened anything.

THE RULE THIS CONFIRMS: when a ratchet goes red in a tree four panes are writing, sample it twice before calling it a finding, and check whether the baseline file is dirty or was committed in the last minute. A pawl firing during someone's legitimate tightening looks identical to a pawl firing on sabotage. The distinguishing evidence is that the second sample disagrees - a real defect persists.

title: refusalScanner credits refusal sites by mention, so a comment naming a code hides the gap it describes
description:
src/testing/refusals/refusalScanner.ts decides how many refusal sites in a file are
tested by COUNTING test blocks that mention each code, then crediting that many sites
in line order (`additionalTested = Math.min(unCitedSites.length, remainingTests)`,
around line 482). Attribution is by quantity, not identity.

## Observed, not theorised

Writing scripts/download-facsimiles.test.ts 21.8 - a comment recording WHY the three
`pdf-parse-failed` throws cannot be tested - dropped the reported untested count for
that file from 7 to 6 and removed the trio from the breakdown entirely. A note whose
whole purpose was to make a gap visible made the gate stop reporting it. Nothing was
tested. Removing the literal (assembling the code from parts) restored all three.

Measured the same tick: download-facsimiles.ts:1115 is credited as tested and is both
unreachable and undriven. It is a duplicate non-HTTPS check below a loadConfig that
already refuses the same case with the same code (see am-<folio>/this commit's 21.7).

## Why it matters beyond bookkeeping

This is the substring-standing-in-for-category class (am-o44v, am-fkyc) inside the gate
built to count unproven refusals. am-fkyc already fixed the file-level half of exactly
this - `content.includes(basename(srcRel))` crediting 37 `session.ts` files from one
mention - and left the code-level half in place. The consequence is worse than a wrong
number: a comment explaining a gap CLOSES the gap in the report.

## The mechanism already exists

The scanner honours explicit `(file.ts:LINE)` citations, scoped to files the test
actually imports (refusalScanner.ts:392-415). That path is identity-based and correct.
All thirteen arms in scripts/download-facsimiles.test.ts 21.x and
scripts/verify-facsimile-pins.test.ts 5b now cite their site, and the pins file's nine
remaining sites are correctly reported after the change.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. A test block that mentions a refusal code without citing a site credits NO site.
   Uncited blocks may still be reported, but as unattributed rather than as coverage.
2. A planted comment naming a code (not in a test block) does not change any count.
   Drive this red first: the 21.8 case above is a known-reachable fixture.
3. The change is a gate diff and ships alone, reviewed separately (AGENTS.md RH-1).
4. Migration: files whose coverage was count-credited will regress when citations
   become mandatory. Report the new true counts before raising any baseline, and
   NEVER raise a baseline to absorb them - the increase is the defect becoming visible.
5. A control proving the citation path still credits: remove one citation and the
   corresponding site returns to the untested list.

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text:
## IMPLEMENTED 53618613 (GreenAnchor), and one follow-on found while doing it

The ruling is in: uncited sites under a multi-site code are never credited; single-site
codes unchanged; repeated codes disclosed in every failing file's report.

MEASURED WITH THE SCANNER, per site, before and after, then diffed:
  before  99 untested of 2120 coded sites
  after  404 untested of 2120
  305 sites LOSE credit, 0 gain. Zero gains is asserted as an invariant, not just observed.

61 files newly over baseline, 23 already over. No baseline touched - owner's call.

## FOLLOW-ON: a stale citation is indistinguishable from no citation

Found by the tightening, in my own work. The seven 5b arms in
scripts/verify-facsimile-pins.test.ts cited lines 700-772. Inserting the extract-folio
evaluator above them moved every site by ~159 lines. Nothing said so, because under the
old mention-credit rule those sites were credited anyway - so the file reported 0 untested
while seven of its citations pointed at nothing.

That means my earlier "16 to 0" for that file was partly luck, and it means the citation
mechanism this ruling now depends on has no integrity check of its own. A mistyped line,
an outdated line, and a deliberate lie are all the same to the scanner: it silently
ignores a citation that matches no site.

Now that citations CARRY credit rather than merely refine it, that gap matters more.

### Acceptance for the follow-on

1. A citation whose (file, line) matches no throw site in that file is REPORTED, naming
   the file, the cited line, and the test file that wrote it. It is a defect in the test,
   not in the source.
2. Do not auto-repair by nearest line. A citation that has drifted is a claim nobody has
   re-checked, and quietly re-pointing it would launder exactly what this bead is about.
3. Plant it: take a valid citation, add a line above the site, confirm the report names
   the now-stale citation. Measured, not argued.
4. Report the count of stale citations across the tree before deciding whether it is a
   hard failure or a disclosure. On 2026-09-21 verify-facsimile-pins.test.ts had 7 of 16
   stale and download-facsimiles.test.ts had 0 of 9; the rest of the tree is unmeasured.

title: Labs silently coerce or accept out-of-domain inputs: SR-08 and SR-12 turn 1e300 into 0c, SR-03/06/12 accept v >= c, BM-01 ignores its 273-330 K domain
description:
## Background

AGENTS.md "Parameter design and constraint handling": out-of-domain inputs are never silently clamped while the label shows the requested value. They explain the problem and offer an admissible boundary or a model change. A scientific result is never NaN, infinity, zero or a silent clamp. Each manifest (content/experiments/<id>.yaml) declares `modelDomain` per control, with a reason.

## What is wrong (measured on live 2026-09-24, typing extreme values into each lab)

- SR-08 and SR-12 turn a typed 1e300 into 0 and report "Accepted ... moving at 0c".
- SR-03, SR-06 and SR-12 give no refusal at all for v >= 1 (in units of c) or for a rest length L0 <= 0.
- BM-01 accepts T = 1e300 K (RMS 5.8e148 µm, one curve silently fails to draw) and 5000 K. Its own manifest says `modelDomain: min 273, max 330, reason "Liquid state of water at ordinary laboratory pressure"`.
- LQ-06 shows readers a raw developer error string.

## What to do

1. Every control in all 33 labs enforces its manifest `modelDomain`, not just its visual range.
   - Outside the domain: the typed outside-domain result, in ordinary language, naming the admissible range and the manifest's reason, keeping the last accepted snapshot visible and clearly distinct from the requested value.
   - No inertial observer at |v| >= c. A rest length must be positive.
2. No raw error string reaches a reader. Each refusal has an ordinary-language explanation and a next action.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A sweep over every numeric control of the 33 labs reports "N of M controls enforce their declared domain", with N = M. It is typed on live with 1e300, -1e300, 0, a value just past each bound, and "abc".
- 0 raw error strings on any lab page under the sweep.
- Planted negatives: removing one lab's domain check lets 1e300 through, and the sweep test goes red.

## Tests

- A shared test helper that reads each manifest's modelDomain and drives the lab's accept path.
- Per-lab negatives.
- Browser check at 390 for three labs.

Dispatch 134 (TopazPrairie) started this.

title: Three labs have no manifest, four have no embed route, and five don't state the question they answer
description:
## Background

AGENTS.md "How to Add an Instrument":
- every instrument has a manifest content/experiments/<id>.yaml, with notModeled filled;
- an embed at /embed/lab/[experiment];
- it states the explanatory question it answers.

## Measured on live and in the repo (2026-09-24)

- No manifest file: lq-02, bm-02, sr-05.
- No embed route (404): lq-02, bm-02, sr-05, me-03.
- The page does not state its question: 5 of 33 (list them from scratchpad/reality/instruments.md, or re-measure).

## What to do

- Author the three manifests from the labs' existing registry and reference owners, with notModeled, domains and acceptance cases.
- Add the four embed routes with attribution and a link back.
- State the question on the five pages.

## Acceptance Criteria

- 33/33 manifests, 33/33 embeds returning 200, and 33/33 pages stating their question, measured on live.
- The instrument audit (see am-instrument-audit-defaults-pass-50bl) passes on real data, not defaults.

## Tests and logging

- Content: the manifest schema validates the three new manifests.
- Browser: the four new embeds return 200 with attribution, and each of the 33 lab pages shows its question.

Structured logs: each suite writes JSON lines to artifacts/test-logs/<suite>/<log-run-id>.jsonl with the AGENTS.md fields that apply (timestamp, suite, logRunId, testId, beadId, paper, anchor, instrumentId, expected, actual, outcome, browser, viewport, jsEnabled, message). A failing browser test keeps a screenshot, trace, DOM snapshot and console log.
